_doc: HMTc Category 23 (Food-Contact Consumer Goods and Kitchenware) compiler config. Method v2.0, government-limit-only. THE NATIVE BASIS OF THIS ENTIRE CATEGORY IS SPECIFIC ELEMENT MIGRATION INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT, in µg/kg of food, per the Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II convention. The register contains exactly ONE instrument family expressed in that basis: the EU 10/2011 Annex II element list (Pb, Cd, tAs and tHg not detectable at their stated detection limits; total Cr not detectable with a 3.6 mg/kg relaxation on documented Cr(VI) exclusion, which HMTc declines; Ni SML 0.02 mg/kg food; Al SML 1 mg/kg food; no tin entry). Every published number on every row in this category traces to that family, either directly where the food-contact surface is a plastic within the instrument's scope, or by a disclosed read-across where the food-contact surface is a polymeric material the instrument expressly excludes (silicone, Art. 2(2)(c); ion-exchange resin, Art. 2(2)(a)) or does not reach (cured liquid-applied coatings and lacquers, a Regulation 1935/2004 Annex I family with no specific measure; paper and board; wood). WHERE THE FOOD-CONTACT SURFACE IS METAL, ALLOY, CERAMIC GLAZE, VITREOUS ENAMEL OR GLASS, THE ROW IS A CONTROL AND NO NUMBER IS INVENTED. That is not a shortcut: the release regimes that actually govern those families are absent from the register (EU Council Directive 84/500/EEC on ceramic articles as amended by 2005/31/EC; the US FDA compliance-policy guides on lead in ceramicware and decorated glassware; California Proposition 65 tableware consent judgments; the Council of Europe metals-and-alloys technical guide; SDWA s.1417 lead-free and NSF/ANSI 61 for water-contact materials; China GB 4806 series), and they are recorded as register gaps rather than replaced with a plastics value. THREE FOREIGN BASES appear in this category only as disclosed companions and are never published as a ceiling: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents of the can and not the can), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS 2024-29 percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals, solder and tin plating; CPSIA total lead in substrate; EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium restrictions; RoHS homogeneous-material limits), and the WATER basis (drinking-water parametric values, which limit the water as delivered and not the device). A fourth basis is excluded outright: the TOY article-extraction basis (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III Categories I to III and ASTM F963 soluble limits) measures element migration from scraped-off or coated toy material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid expressed per kg of MATERIAL, is orders of magnitude looser than a per-kg-of-food migration limit, and is barred from this category by every row's basis_guard. ONE DELIBERATE DEPARTURE from the default convention is recorded here for audit: total chromium is published as a FIRM cell rather than a screen on the 10/2011-anchored rows, because Annex II point 2 sets total chromium at not detectable precisely so that hexavalent chromium need not be assumed absent, and relaxes to 3.6 mg/kg food only on documented Cr(VI) exclusion; the non-detect branch is therefore the Cr(VI)-conservative form of the requirement rather than a Cr(III)-dominated artefact, HMTc declines the relaxation, and the Cr-VI cell is speciation-bounded by it. On the control rows, by contrast, total chromium is a control and its rationale states plainly that it is a screening determination and not a protective ceiling, and Cr-VI is a control rather than a not-material determination because no published parent bounds it there. Species never replace totals anywhere in this category: iAs cannot satisfy tAs, MeHg cannot satisfy tHg, Cr-VI cannot satisfy total Cr.

_category.name: Food-Contact Consumer Goods and Kitchenware
_category.anchor: EU food-contact framework Regulation 1935/2004 with Regulation (EU) 10/2011 Annex II specific migration limits as the only element-migration instrument in the register expressed in the food-contact FOOD basis (the register's other migration instruments — the EU 2009/48 toy Categories I to III and the ASTM F963 soluble limits — are in the toy article-extraction basis and are barred from every row of this category). Rows whose principal food-contact surface is a polymer anchor it directly, or by disclosed read-across where the instrument's own scope article excludes or does not reach the material or where the taxonomy row also carries a non-plastic configuration. Metal, alloy, ceramic-glaze, vitreous-enamel and glass rows, and the two water-treatment-device rows, are controls because their dedicated release regimes (Directive 84/500/EEC as amended by 2005/31/EC, the metals-and-alloys release regime, and the drinking-water device route) are not in the register in their own jurisdictions' rows. Where one taxonomy row carries both a polymer and a metal configuration, the published cells take the metal-article control and the plastics value is disclosed as a film-only companion.
_category.basis_family: Specific element migration INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT, µg/kg of food (Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II convention). Bases are never conflated in this category. A migration ceiling is never published as a content ceiling and a content, food or water ceiling is never published as a migration ceiling. The three foreign bases that surround these rows appear only as disclosed companions: FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, on the contents not the article), MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS 2024-29 percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals, solder and tin plating; CPSIA total lead in substrate; EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium; RoHS homogeneous materials), and WATER basis (drinking-water parametric values, on the water as delivered not the device). The TOY article-extraction basis (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III Categories I to III, ASTM F963 soluble limits, per kg of MATERIAL into 0.07 M HCl) is barred from every row by basis_guard. One further register fact is stated at category level so no row has to be read to find it: the register contains four Uruguayan Reglamento Bromatologico Nacional section 12.5.13 rows (uy_rbn_pb_ceramic_fillable_objects_4mgkg, uy_rbn_cd_ceramic_fillable_objects_0_3mgkg, uy_rbn_pb_cookware_storage_gt3l_1_5mgkg, uy_rbn_cd_cookware_storage_gt3l_0_1mgkg) whose lead and cadmium values for fillable ceramic articles and for ceramic cooking and storage ware over three litres match the EU Category II and Category III release values. They are named and declined in every cell of the six ceramic, vitreous-enamel and glass rows on three stated grounds — Uruguay is outside the credible-regulator set used for anchoring in this build, the register normalises the rows to a per-mass figure while the regime is per volume of extract or per dm2 of surface, and they do not reach the Category I flat and lip-band configuration — rather than being passed over in silence. Absence of the instrument is not asserted anywhere in this standard
_category.method_label: HMTc Method v2.0 (government-limit-only): the strictest applicable sovereign maximum for this exact product form expressed as specific element migration into food or a food simulant; a disclosed read-across from the nearest applicable sovereign value in the same basis where the food-contact material family is expressly excluded from or not reached by that instrument; a substantiated not-material determination; or a control. No cell is occurrence-derived, and no cell borrows a value across a basis.
_category.method_note: TWO CATEGORY RULES govern every row. (1) THE MATERIAL-FAMILY RULE: a row's published ceiling is anchored only where a sovereign instrument governs element migration into food from that row's PRINCIPAL food-contact material family. Polymer surfaces IN THE FOOD BASIS anchor EU 10/2011 Annex II directly, or by disclosed read-across where the instrument expressly excludes the polymer (silicone under Art. 2(2)(c)) or does not reach it (cured liquid-applied coatings, paper and board, wood and bamboo). Ion-exchange resin is expressly excluded by Art. 2(2)(a), but that exclusion generates NO read-across in this category: the only rows on which ion-exchange resin appears are the two water-treatment-device rows, whose native basis is net element release into the treated water, and reading a food-basis migration ceiling across into a treated-water-basis row would be a basis conflation. Resin, housing and every other wetted device component are under the net-device-contribution control instead, with no separate published ceiling. Metal, alloy, ceramic-glaze, vitreous-enamel and glass surfaces have no release ceiling in the register that a row of this category may bind — the credible-set instruments for those families are absent, and the four non-allowlisted Uruguayan ceramic rows that the register does hold are named and declined on stated grounds at row level rather than treated as absent — so those rows are controls with mandatory testing and no invented number. (2) THE COMPONENT RULE: every food-contact COMPONENT of an article is held to the regime of its own material family, and where a component's family has no sovereign ceiling that component is under control. A row's published cells state the ceiling for its principal food-contact material; the component plan names the other components, the regime each falls under, and which component is expected to bind. A result from a non-binding component does not represent the article: a can body wall does not represent its seam, a vacuum bottle wall does not represent its base-plug solder, a plain tumbler does not represent a decorated one, a blender jar does not represent its blade assembly, and a cold reservoir does not represent a post-descaling draw. (3) MIXED-MATERIAL ROWS AND PROVENANCE: where one taxonomy row covers both a configuration the anchoring instrument governs directly and a configuration that instrument expressly excludes or does not reach, the row is published with READ-ACROSS provenance rather than regulatory-alignment. The published number is identical either way; the tag is chosen so the machine-readable provenance never asserts regulatory alignment to an instrument whose own scope article does not reach one of the row's materials, and each cell's label states which configuration is direct and which is read across. The resulting under-description of the directly-governed configuration is deliberate and is the conservative direction. Splitting such a row into two taxonomy rows, each carrying its own basis and provenance, is the exact fix; it is a taxonomy change and is recorded for governance rather than taken unilaterally in this config.

food-packaging-cans-lids.name: Cans/lids
food-packaging-cans-lids.native_basis: specific element migration into food or food simulant (µg/kg food), Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II convention
food-packaging-cans-lids.native_basis_label: specific element migration INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT from the polymeric food-contact surface, µg/kg of food, determined by the Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex III to V simulant, temperature and contact-time conventions. This is a MIGRATION basis and not a total-content basis: no cell on this row limits how much of an element the material CONTAINS, and no cell on this row is expressed per kg of material.
food-packaging-cans-lids.scope_note: The finished sealed can and its end as filled and processed, including hot-fill and retort sterilised product. The food-contact surface of a modern food can is the cured organic interior lacquer, so the published ceilings read across from the plastics migration instrument. Where a can interior is UNCOATED tinplate, or where the lacquer is breached, that configuration falls to the metal-article release control regime instead, and the tin cell is a control on every configuration. Tin is the defining pathway for this row and the canned-food tin maximum levels are a FOOD-basis companion on the contents, disclosed here and never published as this row's migration ceiling.
food-packaging-cans-lids.material: Three-piece or two-piece tinplate or electrolytically chromium-coated steel, or aluminium, with a cured organic interior lacquer (epoxy-phenolic, polyester, acrylic or oleoresinous); welded or, historically, soldered side seam; compound-lined ends.
food-packaging-cans-lids.components: Sample and report separately: (1) interior lacquer on the body wall; (2) interior lacquer on the end panel and the double-seam area, where coating coverage is thinnest; (3) exposed tinplate or chromium-coated steel at the side seam and at score or easy-open features; (4) end-compound sealing gasket; (5) any solder at the side seam on legacy or imported stock; (6) interior printing or coding inks. Report the seam and end-panel result as the binding component; a body-wall-only result does not represent the article.
food-packaging-cans-lids.audit_scope: food.contact|food contact|plastic food|utensil|cookware|cooking utensil|kitchen|tableware|crockery|ceramic|porcelain|earthenware|glaze|enamel|glassware|hollowware|packaging and containers|food-contact surface
food-packaging-cans-lids.basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as specific element migration into food or a food simulant may anchor a cell on this row. The guard exists to reject the three foreign bases that surround this category and would otherwise look plausible: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents and not the article), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (CPSIA total lead in substrate, EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium percent-by-weight restrictions, RoHS homogeneous-material limits, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals), and the ARTICLE-EXTRACTION basis of the toy regime (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III and ASTM F963 soluble limits, which are element migration from scraped-off or coated TOY material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid, expressed per kg of MATERIAL, not per kg of food). Any of those would fail this guard and resolve to a gap rather than publish in the wrong basis. On this control row the guard is declaratory as well as operative: it records the only basis in which a future ingested instrument would be allowed to supply this row's numbers, so that a content limit, a food limit, a water limit or a plastics specific migration limit cannot later be dropped in as this row's release ceiling. The plastics clause is deliberately absent from this guard: a Reg (EU) 10/2011 value named here would fail the guard and resolve to a gap.

read_across.label: read-across of the EU 10/2011 Annex II point 2 lead non-detect requirement (0.01 mg/kg food)
read_across.substantiation: The exact cell is unregulated: the food-contact surface of a food can is a cured organic coating, and coatings and varnishes are a Regulation 1935/2004 Annex I material family for which the EU has adopted no specific measure, while Regulation (EU) 10/2011 reaches plastic layers and plastic coatings in multi-material multi-layer articles but is not written for a liquid-applied cured lacquer. The nearest applicable sovereign value in the identical basis is therefore the EU 10/2011 Annex II element requirement for a polymeric food-contact layer, and it is read across with disclosure. The read-across holds the basis constant: source and destination are the same measured quantity, specific element migration into food or a food simulant in µg/kg food, determined by the same test conventions. The analogy is on basis and exposure endpoint, not on material identity, and it is disclosed as a read-across rather than presented as a limit written for this article. Lead is on the Annex II point 2 not-detectable list, so the published ceiling is the 0.01 mg/kg food detection limit and not a positive migration allowance. Applied to the can, this ceiling governs the lacquered interior surface as the food-contact surface; the uncoated-tinplate and breached-coating configurations are handled by the component plan under the metal-article release control regime, and the tin pathway is a control on every configuration. This is a migration ceiling on the food or simulant and is never reported as a limit on the material's lead content; the material-content instruments (US CPSIA total lead in children's-product substrate, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS 2024-29 percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals and solder) are separate obligations in a different basis and are not this cell.

control.rationale: Regulation (EU) 10/2011 Annex II lists no tin entry, and no credible sovereign sets a tin migration or release ceiling for a can, a can end or any other food-contact article. Tin is the defining pathway of this row, so a control here is a mandatory determination and not a shrug: tin dissolves from exposed tinplate wherever the interior lacquer is absent, thin or breached, which is why the sovereign response to canned-food tin is a maximum level on the FOOD rather than on the article. Those food maximum levels (EU Reg 2023/915 at 200 mg/kg for canned foods and 100 mg/kg for canned beverages, Codex CXS 193 and FSANZ Schedule 19 at 250 mg/kg, and 50 mg/kg for canned infant and young-child products) are disclosed as a companion obligation on the contents. They are a FOOD basis, they are measured in the food and not in a simulant against the article, and republishing one of them as this row's migration ceiling would be the exact basis conflation this category's guard exists to prevent.
control.reference_method: EN 1186 / EN 13130 food-simulant migration testing on the finished article under its worst foreseeable use conditions (simulant, temperature and contact time selected per Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex III and Annex V; for repeat-use articles the third successive migration result governs), with ICP-MS determination of the element in the simulant. Tin determined additionally on the finished packed product at the end of the declared shelf life, and on the seam and end-panel extraction separately, because tin dissolution is progressive and localised.

The analogy is on basis and exposure endpoint, not on material identity, and it is disclosed as a read-across rather than presented as a limit written for this article. Aluminium carries a positive specific migration limit of 1 mg/kg food, added by Reg (EU) 2016/1416. food-packaging-cans-lids.cross_reference: Category 9 (Infant and Child Contact Products) governs any article in this row that is marketed for ages 0-5; the taxonomy boundary rule routes infant bottles, nipples and toddler drinkware there even though they are food-contact items.

food-packaging-glass-jars.name: Glass jars
food-packaging-glass-jars.native_basis: element release from the glaze, vitreous enamel or glass into food or food simulant, declared in TWO native bases: ug/dm2 of food-contact surface for non-fillable and shallow articles and for decoration within 20 mm of the lip (Directive 84/500/EEC Category I convention), and ug/L of 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid extract for fillable articles (Category II) and for articles over three litres and cooking ware (Category III), reportable as ug/kg only on the explicitly stated 1 L = 1 kg convention
food-packaging-glass-jars.native_basis_label: element RELEASE FROM THE GLAZE, VITREOUS ENAMEL OR GLASS NETWORK INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT, declared in TWO NATIVE BASES because the governing release regime is written in two and this row never merges them. BASIS A, for non-fillable and shallow articles and for any decoration lying within 20 mm of the lip: ug per dm2 of food-contact surface, the Directive 84/500/EEC Category I convention. BASIS B, for fillable articles (Category II) and for articles over three litres and cooking ware (Category III): ug per litre of 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid extract, reportable as ug/kg ONLY on the explicitly stated 1 L = 1 kg convention, which is the single unit conversion this row permits. CONVERSION OF A PER-AREA RESULT INTO A PER-MASS OR PER-VOLUME RESULT IS FORBIDDEN on this row: it requires a food-contact-area-per-kg-of-food assumption (the occurrence literature commonly uses 5 dm2 per kg of foodstuff) that this standard does not adopt, and adopting it would smuggle an unstated assumption into a certification number. Every result is reported in the basis its article form generates, and a per-dm2 result and a per-litre result are never pooled, averaged or compared. This is a RELEASE basis and not a total-content basis, and it is deliberately NOT the Reg (EU) 10/2011 plastics-simulant convention: a plastics specific migration limit is never substituted for a release limit on this family.
food-packaging-glass-jars.scope_note: The glass container as filled, together with its closure system. The principal food-contact material is the glass network, whose element release regime is not present in the register as rows of its own jurisdiction; the only register rows carrying release numbers for this article family are four non-allowlisted Uruguayan rows, named and declined on stated grounds in every cell. The row is a control. The closure's plasticised sealing compound is a plastic gasket in a cap or closure and is directly within Reg (EU) 10/2011 Art. 2(1)(d), so that component is bound by the plastics migration ceilings as a companion obligation reported under the caps-and-closures row; the metal closure shell falls to the metal-article release control regime. TRACEABILITY OF THE COMPONENT POINTER: where this row's component plan refers a plastic component to "the plastics migration ceilings", that phrase resolves to a concrete published set of values inside this same standard and is not an unresolved pointer. It means the Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II values published on this category's plastics rows — eu_10_2011_pb_sml_nd (lead, not detectable at 10 ug/kg food), eu_10_2011_cd_sml_nd (cadmium, 2), eu_10_2011_tas_sml_nd (total arsenic, 10), eu_10_2011_thg_sml_nd (total mercury, 10), eu_10_2011_ni_sml (nickel, 20), eu_10_2011_al_sml (aluminium, 1000) and eu_10_2011_crtotal_sml_nd (total chromium, not detectable at 10), with tin excepted because the instrument lists no tin entry. Those values bind the plastic component as a SEPARATE obligation in its own material family and are never this row's published ceiling, which stays in this row's own native basis.

food-packaging-glass-jars.basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as element RELEASE from a glaze, vitreous-enamel or glass food-contact surface into food, a food simulant or the 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid extract convention, per dm2 of food-contact surface or per litre of extract, may anchor a cell on this row. The guard exists to reject the three foreign bases that surround this category and would otherwise look plausible: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents and not the article), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (CPSIA total lead in substrate, EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium percent-by-weight restrictions, RoHS homogeneous-material limits, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals), and the ARTICLE-EXTRACTION basis of the toy regime (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III and ASTM F963 soluble limits, which are element migration from scraped-off or coated TOY material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid, expressed per kg of MATERIAL, not per kg of food). Any of those would fail this guard and resolve to a gap rather than publish in the wrong basis. On this control row the guard is declaratory as well as operative: it records the only basis in which a future ingested instrument would be allowed to supply this row's numbers, so that a content limit, a food limit, a water limit or a plastics specific migration limit cannot later be dropped in as this row's release ceiling. The plastics clause is deliberately absent from this guard: a Reg (EU) 10/2011 value named here would fail the guard and resolve to a gap. DECLARED VACUOUS STATE (recorded, not overlooked): as written this guard matches ZERO live, non-draft and non-quarantined rows in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv, and that is its intended state. The release regime this row's basis family belongs to is not in the register in any form this row may bind, which is the same fact this row's control cells record and state in detail; a guard that admitted a live row today could only do so by admitting a foreign basis. The guard is nevertheless expressed in the register's own basis vocabulary (element or specific release, release into food or a food simulant, 4 percent acetic acid extract, per dm2 of food-contact surface, net device contribution to the treated water) so that a future correct ingest of that regime BINDS through it. The previous prose-sentence guard on this row would have REJECTED the very instruments it was waiting for and forced them to a gap, which is the defect this rewrite removes. Two limits on the guard's force are stated plainly rather than left implicit: the compiler returns on the control branch before basis resolution, so a guard is never evaluated on a control cell, and this note rather than the machine is what carries the guard's force on this row today. control.rationale: No credible sovereign release ceiling for this material family is available to anchor this cell, and the register position is stated exactly rather than by assertion of absence. The regime that governs this material family in the real world is EU Council Directive 84/500/EEC as amended by Directive 2005/31/EC, supported in the United States by the FDA compliance-policy guides on lead in ceramicware and decorated glassware and by the California Proposition 65 tableware consent judgments; none of those instruments is present in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv as a row of its own jurisdiction, and each is recorded as a register gap for ingest through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway. What the register DOES hold for this exact article class is named here rather than passed over: four Uruguayan Reglamento Bromatologico Nacional section 12.5.13 rows carrying the same numbers as the EU Category II and Category III release values, namely uy_rbn_pb_ceramic_fillable_objects_4mgkg (lead, 4000 ug/kg) and uy_rbn_cd_ceramic_fillable_objects_0_3mgkg (cadmium, 300 ug/kg), both scoped to food-contact ceramic objects that can be filled, and uy_rbn_pb_cookware_storage_gt3l_1_5mgkg (lead, 1500 ug/kg) and uy_rbn_cd_cookware_storage_gt3l_0_1mgkg (cadmium, 100 ug/kg), both scoped to ceramic cooking utensils, packaging and storage containers with capacity over three litres. Those four rows are DECLINED on three stated grounds, and not because they are absent. First, Uruguay sits OUTSIDE the HMTc credible-regulator set used for anchoring in this build, so it cannot supply a published number without a recorded governance ruling; this is the same treatment already given on the metal rows to Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS Notice 2024-29, and it is a jurisdictional gate rather than a judgement about Uruguayan law. Second, the register normalises those rows to a per-MASS figure carrying basis_class as_sold, while the regime they transcribe is expressed per volume of 4 percent acetic acid extract for fillable articles and per unit of food-contact surface area for flat and shallow ones, so binding them would publish a number in a basis the register row does not resolve. Third, they reach only the fillable (Category II) and over-three-litre and cooking-ware (Category III) configurations; no register row covers the Category I flat, shallow and lip-band configuration, which on a decorated plate or a drinking-vessel rim is the higher-release configuration and the one a ceiling would most need to govern. This build separately refuses to substitute the plastics specific migration limits for a glaze-release limit: the two are different extractions on different material families and the substitution would be a basis conflation. The cell is therefore a control with mandatory release testing and no invented number until 84/500/EEC as amended is ingested in its own EU rows and native bases. Lead is the dominant pathway for this material family: lead-fluxed and lead-bisilicate glazes, lead-bearing on-glaze enamels and applied decoration, and under-fired or acid-attacked glaze surfaces all release lead into acidic food. It is the single cell where the absent release regime matters most, and the gap is recorded rather than papered over with a plastics value. On a glass jar the tin route is the TINPLATE CLOSURE SHELL rather than the glass, and the canned-food tin maximum levels are a FOOD-basis companion on the packed contents that is never published as this row's release ceiling. For a glass jar the release surface is the glass network itself and the applied-decoration surface where present; the closure gasket and the closure shell are separate components with their own regimes, recorded in the component plan and never averaged into this row's result.
control.reference_method: Release testing on the filled or contact-surface article using 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid at the article's stated use temperature and duration (the release convention used for glazed, enamelled and glass food-contact articles), ICP-MS determination in the extract, with a separate determination on any decoration lying within 20 mm of the lip or on any interior decoration. Each result is reported in the native basis its article form generates and in no other: per dm2 of food-contact surface for a non-fillable or shallow article and for the decoration band within 20 mm of the lip, and per litre of extract (reportable as ug/kg on the stated 1 L = 1 kg convention) for a fillable article and for an article over three litres or intended for cooking. A per-dm2 result is never converted to a per-mass or per-volume result, and per-area and per-volume results are never pooled.

food-packaging-foils-wraps.native_basis: element release from the food-contact surface into food or food simulant (ug/kg food), reported separately for the polymeric-film and the rolled-aluminium-foil configuration
food-packaging-foils-wraps.native_basis_label: element RELEASE FROM THE FOOD-CONTACT SURFACE INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT, ug/kg of food, determined against acidic and salted simulants at the maximum contact temperature and duration claimed on the pack. The row's PUBLISHED cells are expressed in the METAL-ARTICLE release basis, because one of this row's two configurations is rolled aluminium foil, whose food-contact surface is the element itself and which has no polymeric food-contact surface at all. The Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex III to V plastics-simulant convention governs only the polymeric cling and barrier-film configuration and appears on this row as a disclosed COMPANION obligation, never as the published ceiling for the metal article. This is a RELEASE basis on the food and never a total-content basis: no cell on this row limits how much of an element the material CONTAINS, and no cell is expressed per kg of material.
food-packaging-foils-wraps.scope_note: Two material configurations sit in one taxonomy row and this record holds them apart rather than pooling them. The polymeric cling and barrier-wrap configuration is a material consisting exclusively of plastics and is directly within Reg (EU) 10/2011. The ROLLED ALUMINIUM FOIL configuration is not: it is a metal article whose food-contact surface is the element itself, metals and alloys are a Regulation 1935/2004 Annex I material family for which the EU has adopted no specific measure, and no credible sovereign sets an element release ceiling for a metal foil. Because one taxonomy row can carry only one published provenance, EVERY published cell on this row now takes the METAL-ARTICLE RELEASE CONTROL regime used on cookware-metal-alloy and utensils-metal, and the corresponding Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II value is disclosed as that cell's COMPANION obligation, binding the polymeric-film configuration only and verified on every film lot. This is exactly the treatment aluminium already received on this row, and the reason generalises to every element on the panel: applying a plastics specific migration limit to rolled aluminium foil asserts of an article made of the element a number written for a polymer surface, which is a misapplication rather than a conservative reading, and aluminium foil in contact with acidic and salted food is documented to exceed it. Extending the carve-out to the whole panel moves in the conservative direction, because it declines to publish a ceiling one configuration cannot meet rather than declining to be strict, and it removes the internal contradiction of a record that made the misapplication argument for one element while publishing the misapplication for six. The film and foil configurations are tested, reported and certified separately and are never pooled. Splitting this taxonomy row into a polymeric-wrap row and an aluminium-foil row, each with its own native basis and its own provenance, is the cleaner fix and is recorded as a taxonomy change for governance rather than taken unilaterally here.

food-storage-glass-containers.name: Glass food storage containers
food-storage-glass-containers.native_basis: element release from the glaze, vitreous enamel or glass into food or food simulant, declared in TWO native bases: ug/dm2 of food-contact surface for non-fillable and shallow articles and for decoration within 20 mm of the lip (Directive 84/500/EEC Category I convention), and ug/L of 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid extract for fillable articles (Category II) and for articles over three litres and cooking ware (Category III), reportable as ug/kg only on the explicitly stated 1 L = 1 kg convention
food-storage-glass-containers.native_basis_label: element RELEASE FROM THE GLAZE, VITREOUS ENAMEL OR GLASS NETWORK INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT, declared in TWO NATIVE BASES because the governing release regime is written in two and this row never merges them. BASIS A, for non-fillable and shallow articles and for any decoration lying within 20 mm of the lip: ug per dm2 of food-contact surface, the Directive 84/500/EEC Category I convention. BASIS B, for fillable articles (Category II) and for articles over three litres and cooking ware (Category III): ug per litre of 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid extract, reportable as ug/kg ONLY on the explicitly stated 1 L = 1 kg convention, which is the single unit conversion this row permits. CONVERSION OF A PER-AREA RESULT INTO A PER-MASS OR PER-VOLUME RESULT IS FORBIDDEN on this row: it requires a food-contact-area-per-kg-of-food assumption (the occurrence literature commonly uses 5 dm2 per kg of foodstuff) that this standard does not adopt, and adopting it would smuggle an unstated assumption into a certification number. Every result is reported in the basis its article form generates, and a per-dm2 result and a per-litre result are never pooled, averaged or compared. This is a RELEASE basis and not a total-content basis, and it is deliberately NOT the Reg (EU) 10/2011 plastics-simulant convention: a plastics specific migration limit is never substituted for a release limit on this family.
food-storage-glass-containers.scope_note: The principal food-contact material is the glass network, whose release regime is not present in the register as rows of its own jurisdiction; the only register rows carrying release numbers for this article family are four non-allowlisted Uruguayan rows, named and declined on stated grounds in every cell. The row is a control. Lids and gaskets are separate components under their own regimes. Oven-to-table and freezer-to-oven claims extend the contact conditions and must be tested at the claimed extremes, because release from a glass surface is temperature-dependent. TRACEABILITY OF THE COMPONENT POINTER: where this row's component plan refers a plastic component to "the plastics migration ceilings", that phrase resolves to a concrete published set of values inside this same standard and is not an unresolved pointer. It means the Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II values published on this category's plastics rows — eu_10_2011_pb_sml_nd (lead, not detectable at 10 ug/kg food), eu_10_2011_cd_sml_nd (cadmium, 2), eu_10_2011_tas_sml_nd (total arsenic, 10), eu_10_2011_thg_sml_nd (total mercury, 10), eu_10_2011_ni_sml (nickel, 20), eu_10_2011_al_sml (aluminium, 1000) and eu_10_2011_crtotal_sml_nd (total chromium, not detectable at 10), with tin excepted because the instrument lists no tin entry. Those values bind the plastic component as a SEPARATE obligation in its own material family and are never this row's published ceiling, which stays in this row's own native basis.
food-storage-glass-containers.material: Soda-lime or borosilicate glass bodies, frequently with a plastic lid and a silicone gasket, and often with printed exterior graduations or decoration.
food-storage-glass-containers.components: Sample and report separately: (1) interior glass surface, filled-article extraction at the highest claimed use temperature; (2) plastic lid food-contact face, bound by the plastics migration ceilings; (3) silicone gasket, bound by the plastics ceilings by disclosed read-across; (4) printed exterior graduation or decoration, tested where it lies within 20 mm of the lip; (5) any interior decoration or fill-line print, tested as a decoration.

food-storage-glass-containers.basis_guard: element release|specific release|release into food|release into a food simulant|release into the food simulant|acetic acid|food-contact surface area|mg/dm2|per dm2
food-storage-glass-containers.basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as element RELEASE from a glaze, vitreous-enamel or glass food-contact surface into food, a food simulant or the 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid extract convention, per dm2 of food-contact surface or per litre of extract, may anchor a cell on this row. The guard exists to reject the three foreign bases that surround this category and would otherwise look plausible: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents and not the article), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (CPSIA total lead in substrate, EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium percent-by-weight restrictions, RoHS homogeneous-material limits, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals), and the ARTICLE-EXTRACTION basis of the toy regime (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III and ASTM F963 soluble limits, which are element migration from scraped-off or coated TOY material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid, expressed per kg of MATERIAL, not per kg of food). Any of those would fail this guard and resolve to a gap rather than publish in the wrong basis. On this control row the guard is declaratory as well as operative: it records the only basis in which a future ingested instrument would be allowed to supply this row's numbers, so that a content limit, a food limit, a water limit or a plastics specific migration limit cannot later be dropped in as this row's release ceiling. The plastics clause is deliberately absent from this guard: a Reg (EU) 10/2011 value named here would fail the guard and resolve to a gap. DECLARED VACUOUS STATE (recorded, not overlooked): as written this guard matches ZERO live, non-draft and non-quarantined rows in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv, and that is its intended state. The release regime this row's basis family belongs to is not in the register in any form this row may bind, which is the same fact this row's control cells record and state in detail; a guard that admitted a live row today could only do so by admitting a foreign basis. The guard is nevertheless expressed in the register's own basis vocabulary (element or specific release, release into food or a food simulant, 4 percent acetic acid extract, per dm2 of food-contact surface, net device contribution to the treated water) so that a future correct ingest of that regime BINDS through it. The previous prose-sentence guard on this row would have REJECTED the very instruments it was waiting for and forced them to a gap, which is the defect this rewrite removes. Two limits on the guard's force are stated plainly rather than left implicit: the compiler returns on the control branch before basis resolution, so a guard is never evaluated on a control cell, and this note rather than the machine is what carries the guard's force on this row today. The engine change that would close that hole - an assertion that every declared basis_guard either matches at least one live register row or carries basis_guard_vacuous_by_design, failing the build otherwise - is recorded as a tooling gap and is outside this config's scope.

control.rationale: No credible sovereign release ceiling for this material family is available to anchor this cell, and the register position is stated exactly rather than by assertion of absence. The regime that governs this material family in the real world is EU Council Directive 84/500/EEC as amended by Directive 2005/31/EC, supported in the United States by the FDA compliance-policy guides on lead in ceramicware and decorated glassware and by the California Proposition 65 tableware consent judgments; none of those instruments is present in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv as a row of its own jurisdiction, and each is recorded as a register gap for ingest through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway. What the register DOES hold for this exact article class is named here rather than passed over: four Uruguayan Reglamento Bromatologico Nacional section 12.5.13 rows carrying the same numbers as the EU Category II and Category III release values, namely uy_rbn_pb_ceramic_fillable_objects_4mgkg (lead, 4000 ug/kg) and uy_rbn_cd_ceramic_fillable_objects_0_3mgkg (cadmium, 300 ug/kg), both scoped to food-contact ceramic objects that can be filled, and uy_rbn_pb_cookware_storage_gt3l_1_5mgkg (lead, 1500 ug/kg) and uy_rbn_cd_cookware_storage_gt3l_0_1mgkg (cadmium, 100 ug/kg), both scoped to ceramic cooking utensils, packaging and storage containers with capacity over three litres. Those four rows are DECLINED on three stated grounds, and not because they are absent. First, Uruguay sits OUTSIDE the HMTc credible-regulator set used for anchoring in this build, so it cannot supply a published number without a recorded governance ruling; this is the same treatment already given on the metal rows to Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS Notice 2024-29, and it is a jurisdictional gate rather than a judgement about Uruguayan law. Second, the register normalises those rows to a per-MASS figure carrying basis_class as_sold, while the regime they transcribe is expressed per volume of 4 percent acetic acid extract for fillable articles and per unit of food-contact surface area for flat and shallow ones, so binding them would publish a number in a basis the register row does not resolve. Third, they reach only the fillable (Category II) and over-three-litre and cooking-ware (Category III) configurations; no register row covers the Category I flat, shallow and lip-band configuration, which on a decorated plate or a drinking-vessel rim is the higher-release configuration and the one a ceiling would most need to govern. This build separately refuses to substitute the plastics specific migration limits for a glaze-release limit: the two are different extractions on different material families and the substitution would be a basis conflation. The cell is therefore a control with mandatory release testing and no invented number until 84/500/EEC as amended is ingested in its own EU rows and native bases. Lead is the dominant pathway for this material family: lead-fluxed and lead-bisilicate glazes, lead-bearing on-glaze enamels and applied decoration, and under-fired or acid-attacked glaze surfaces all release lead into acidic food. It is the single cell where the absent release regime matters most, and the gap is recorded rather than papered over with a plastics value. On a glass storage container the release surface is the glass network and any interior or near-lip decoration; the lid and gasket are separate polymer components with their own published ceilings, reported separately and never averaged into this row's result.
control.reference_method: Release testing on the filled or contact-surface article using 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid at the article's stated use temperature and duration (the release convention used for glazed, enamelled and glass food-contact articles), ICP-MS determination in the extract, with a separate determination on any decoration lying within 20 mm of the lip or on any interior decoration. Each result is reported in the native basis its article form generates and in no other: per dm2 of food-contact surface for a non-fillable or shallow article and for the decoration band within 20 mm of the lip, and per litre of extract (reportable as ug/kg on the stated 1 L = 1 kg convention) for a fillable article and for an article over three litres or intended for cooking. A per-dm2 result is never converted to a per-mass or per-volume result, and per-area and per-volume results are never pooled.

food-storage-glass-containers.cross_reference: Category 9 (Infant and Child Contact Products) governs any article in this row that is marketed for ages 0-5; the taxonomy boundary rule routes infant bottles, nipples and toddler drinkware there even though they are food-contact items.

food-storage-silicone.name: Silicone food storage
food-storage-silicone.native_basis: specific element migration into food or food simulant (µg/kg food), Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II convention
food-storage-silicone.native_basis_label: specific element migration INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT from the polymeric food-contact surface, µg/kg of food, determined by the Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex III to V simulant, temperature and contact-time conventions. This is a MIGRATION basis and not a total-content basis: no cell on this row limits how much of an element the material CONTAINS, and no cell on this row is expressed per kg of material.
food-storage-silicone.scope_note: Silicone elastomers are EXPRESSLY EXCLUDED from Reg (EU) 10/2011 by its Art. 2(2)(c), and the EU has adopted no specific measure for silicones under Regulation 1935/2004 Annex I. The exact cell is therefore unregulated, and the published ceilings are a disclosed read-across from the plastics instrument, which is the nearest applicable sovereign value in the identical basis. Because these are repeat-use articles the third successive migration governs; freezer, oven, microwave and steam claims extend the contact conditions and must be tested at the claimed extremes.
food-storage-silicone.material: Platinum- or peroxide-cured polydimethylsiloxane elastomer bags, lids, stretch covers and collapsible containers, with pigment and filler (commonly fumed or precipitated silica, sometimes titanium dioxide or iron oxide colourants).
food-storage-silicone.components: Sample and report separately: (1) elastomer food-contact surface at the third successive migration; (2) pigment and filler masterbatch, verified for lead chromate, cadmium pigment and chrome-green content; (3) any bonded rigid frame, closure or zip component; (4) any metal stiffener, wire or magnet, which falls to the metal-article control regime; (5) printed or embossed branding on a food-contact face.
food-storage-silicone.audit_scope: food.contact|food contact|plastic food|utensil|cookware|cooking utensil|kitchen|tableware|crockery|ceramic|porcelain|earthenware|glaze|enamel|glassware|hollowware|packaging and containers|food-contact surface
food-storage-silicone.basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as specific element migration into food or a food simulant may anchor a cell on this row. The guard exists to reject the three foreign bases that surround this category and would otherwise look plausible: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents and not the article), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (CPSIA total lead in substrate, EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium percent-by-weight restrictions, RoHS homogeneous-material limits, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals), and the ARTICLE-EXTRACTION basis of the toy regime (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III and ASTM F963 soluble limits, which are element migration from scraped-off or coated TOY material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid, expressed per kg of MATERIAL, not per kg of food). Any of those would fail this guard and resolve to a gap rather than publish in the wrong basis.

read_across.label: read-across of the EU 10/2011 Annex II point 2 lead non-detect requirement (0.01 mg/kg food)
read_across.substantiation: The exact cell is unregulated by construction rather than by omission: Reg (EU) 10/2011 Art. 2(2)(c) expressly excludes silicones from its scope, and no EU specific measure and no other credible sovereign instrument sets an element migration ceiling for a silicone food-contact article. The nearest applicable sovereign value is the EU 10/2011 Annex II element requirement for a polymeric food-contact material, read across with disclosure. The read-across holds the basis constant: source and destination are the same measured quantity, specific element migration into food or a food simulant in µg/kg food, determined by the same test conventions. The analogy is on basis and exposure endpoint, not on material identity, and it is disclosed as a read-across rather than presented as a limit written for this article. Lead is on the Annex II point 2 not-detectable list, so the published ceiling is the 0.01 mg/kg food detection limit and not a positive migration allowance. The read-across is tight here: source and destination are both synthetic-polymer repeat-use food-contact articles tested by the same simulant conventions, and the only difference is that the destination polymer was carved out of the instrument's scope for reasons unrelated to element migration. tableware-ceramicware.native_basis_label: element RELEASE FROM THE GLAZE, VITREOUS ENAMEL OR GLASS NETWORK INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT, declared in TWO NATIVE BASES because the governing release regime is written in two and this row never merges them. BASIS A, for non-fillable and shallow articles and for any decoration lying within 20 mm of the lip: ug per dm2 of food-contact surface, the Directive 84/500/EEC Category I convention. BASIS B, for fillable articles (Category II) and for articles over three litres and cooking ware (Category III): ug per litre of 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid extract, reportable as ug/kg ONLY on the explicitly stated 1 L = 1 kg convention, which is the single unit conversion this row permits. CONVERSION OF A PER-AREA RESULT INTO A PER-MASS OR PER-VOLUME RESULT IS FORBIDDEN on this row: it requires a food-contact-area-per-kg-of-food assumption (the occurrence literature commonly uses 5 dm2 per kg of foodstuff) that this standard does not adopt, and adopting it would smuggle an unstated assumption into a certification number. Every result is reported in the basis its article form generates, and a per-dm2 result and a per-litre result are never pooled, averaged or compared. This is a RELEASE basis and not a total-content basis, and it is deliberately NOT the Reg (EU) 10/2011 plastics-simulant convention: a plastics specific migration limit is never substituted for a release limit on this family.
tableware-ceramicware.scope_note: Glazed ceramic food-contact articles: plates, bowls, mugs, serving and cooking ware. This is the highest-risk row in the category and the one where the register gap bites hardest, because the dedicated lead-and-cadmium release regime for ceramic articles (EU Council Directive 84/500/EEC as amended by 2005/31/EC, and the US FDA compliance-policy guide on lead in ceramicware, together with the California Proposition 65 tableware consent judgments) is not present in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv as rows of its own jurisdiction. The only register rows carrying those numbers for this article class are four non-allowlisted Uruguayan Reglamento Bromatologico Nacional section 12.5.13 rows, which are named in full and declined on stated grounds in every cell of this row rather than passed over in silence. The row is a control, the gap is recorded, and the plastics migration limits are NOT substituted: a 4 percent acetic acid glaze-release extraction and a food-simulant plastics migration test are different extractions on different material families, and equating them would be a basis conflation.
tableware-ceramicware.material: Earthenware, stoneware, porcelain and bone china bodies with fired glaze; on-glaze and in-glaze enamel decoration; imported and artisanal ware with lead-fluxed or lead-bisilicate glaze; unglazed or under-fired interior surfaces.
tableware-ceramicware.components: Sample and report separately: (1) interior glazed food-contact surface, filled-article extraction; (2) lip and rim band, including any decoration within 20 mm of the lip; (3) on-glaze or in-glaze enamel decoration on any interior surface; (4) unglazed foot ring, crazed or crawled glaze areas, and any repair or touch-up; (5) handle and spout joins where glaze pools or thins; (6) each glaze and enamel colour as its own lot, because glaze release is colour-specific and a single-colour result does not represent a decorated range.

tableware-ceramicware.basis_guard: element release|specific release|release into food|release into a food simulant|release into the food simulant|acetic acid|food-contact surface area|mg/dm2|per dm2
tableware-ceramicware.basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as element RELEASE from a glaze, vitreous-enamel or glass food-contact surface into food, a food simulant or the 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid extract convention, per dm2 of food-contact surface or per litre of extract, may anchor a cell on this row. The guard exists to reject the three foreign bases that surround this category and would otherwise look plausible: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents and not the article), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (CPSIA total lead in substrate, EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium percent-by-weight restrictions, RoHS homogeneous-material limits, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals), and the ARTICLE-EXTRACTION basis of the toy regime (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III and ASTM F963 soluble limits, which are element migration from scraped-off or coated TOY material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid, expressed per kg of MATERIAL, not per kg of food). Any of those would fail this guard and resolve to a gap rather than publish in the wrong basis. On this control row the guard is declaratory as well as operative: it records the only basis in which a future ingested instrument would be allowed to supply this row's numbers, so that a content limit, a food limit, a water limit or a plastics specific migration limit cannot later be dropped in as this row's release ceiling. The plastics clause is deliberately absent from this guard: a Reg (EU) 10/2011 value named here would fail the guard and resolve to a gap. DECLARED VACUOUS STATE (recorded, not overlooked): as written this guard matches ZERO live, non-draft and non-quarantined rows in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv, and that is its intended state. The release regime this row's basis family belongs to is not in the register in any form this row may bind, which is the same fact this row's control cells record and state in detail; a guard that admitted a live row today could only do so by admitting a foreign basis. The guard is nevertheless expressed in the register's own basis vocabulary (element or specific release, release into food or a food simulant, 4 percent acetic acid extract, per dm2 of food-contact surface, net device contribution to the treated water) so that a future correct ingest of that regime BINDS through it. The previous prose-sentence guard on this row would have REJECTED the very instruments it was waiting for and forced them to a gap, which is the defect this rewrite removes. Two limits on the guard's force are stated plainly rather than left implicit: the compiler returns on the control branch before basis resolution, so a guard is never evaluated on a control cell, and this note rather than the machine is what carries the guard's force on this row today. The engine change that would close that hole - an assertion that every declared basis_guard either matches at least one live register row or carries basis_guard_vacuous_by_design, failing the build otherwise - is recorded as a tooling gap and is outside this config's scope.

control.rationale: No credible sovereign release ceiling for this material family is available to anchor this cell, and the register position is stated exactly rather than by assertion of absence. The regime that governs this material family in the real world is EU Council Directive 84/500/EEC as amended by Directive 2005/31/EC, supported in the United States by the FDA compliance-policy guides on lead in ceramicware and decorated glassware and by the California Proposition 65 tableware consent judgments; none of those instruments is present in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv as a row of its own jurisdiction, and each is recorded as a register gap for ingest through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway. What the register DOES hold for this exact article class is named here rather than passed over: four Uruguayan Reglamento Bromatologico Nacional section 12.5.13 rows carrying the same numbers as the EU Category II and Category III release values, namely uy_rbn_pb_ceramic_fillable_objects_4mgkg (lead, 4000 ug/kg) and uy_rbn_cd_ceramic_fillable_objects_0_3mgkg (cadmium, 300 ug/kg), both scoped to food-contact ceramic objects that can be filled, and uy_rbn_pb_cookware_storage_gt3l_1_5mgkg (lead, 1500 ug/kg) and uy_rbn_cd_cookware_storage_gt3l_0_1mgkg (cadmium, 100 ug/kg), both scoped to ceramic cooking utensils, packaging and storage containers with capacity over three litres. Those four rows are DECLINED on three stated grounds, and not because they are absent. First, Uruguay sits OUTSIDE the HMTc credible-regulator set used for anchoring in this build, so it cannot supply a published number without a recorded governance ruling; this is the same treatment already given on the metal rows to Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS Notice 2024-29, and it is a jurisdictional gate rather than a judgement about Uruguayan law. Second, the register normalises those rows to a per-MASS figure carrying basis_class as_sold, while the regime they transcribe is expressed per volume of 4 percent acetic acid extract for fillable articles and per unit of food-contact surface area for flat and shallow ones, so binding them would publish a number in a basis the register row does not resolve. Third, they reach only the fillable (Category II) and over-three-litre and cooking-ware (Category III) configurations; no register row covers the Category I flat, shallow and lip-band configuration, which on a decorated plate or a drinking-vessel rim is the higher-release configuration and the one a ceiling would most need to govern. This build separately refuses to substitute the plastics specific migration limits for a glaze-release limit: the two are different extractions on different material families and the substitution would be a basis conflation. The cell is therefore a control with mandatory release testing and no invented number until 84/500/EEC as amended is ingested in its own EU rows and native bases. Lead is the dominant pathway for this material family: lead-fluxed and lead-bisilicate glazes, lead-bearing on-glaze enamels and applied decoration, and under-fired or acid-attacked glaze surfaces all release lead into acidic food. It is the single cell where the absent release regime matters most, and the gap is recorded rather than papered over with a plastics value. Ceramicware is the row for which the absent release regime is most consequential, so the control is written to be operative: every glaze and enamel colour is tested as its own lot, the lip band is tested separately, and a detection triggers escalation rather than a comparison against a borrowed number.
control.reference_method: Release testing on the filled or contact-surface article using 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid at the article's stated use temperature and duration (the release convention used for glazed, enamelled and glass food-contact articles), ICP-MS determination in the extract, with a separate determination on any decoration lying within 20 mm of the lip or on any interior decoration. Each result is reported in the native basis its article form generates and in no other: per dm2 of food-contact surface for a non-fillable or shallow article and for the decoration band within 20 mm of the lip, and per litre of extract (reportable as ug/kg on the stated 1 L = 1 kg convention) for a fillable article and for an article over three litres or intended for cooking. A per-dm2 result is never converted to a per-mass or per-volume result, and per-area and per-volume results are never pooled.

What the register DOES hold for this exact article class is named here rather than passed over: four Uruguayan Reglamento Bromatologico Nacional section 12.5.13 rows carrying the same numbers as the EU Category II and Category III release values, namely uy_rbn_pb_ceramic_fillable_objects_4mgkg (lead, 4000 ug/kg) and uy_rbn_cd_ceramic_fillable_objects_0_3mgkg (cadmium, 300 ug/kg), both scoped to food-contact ceramic objects that can be filled, and uy_rbn_pb_cookware_storage_gt3l_1_5mgkg (lead, 1500 ug/kg) and uy_rbn_cd_cookware_storage_gt3l_0_1mgkg (cadmium, 100 ug/kg), both scoped to ceramic cooking utensils, packaging and storage containers with capacity over three litres. Those four rows are DECLINED on three stated grounds, and not because they are absent. First, Uruguay sits OUTSIDE the HMTc credible-regulator set used for anchoring in this build, so it cannot supply a published number without a recorded governance ruling; this is the same treatment already given on the metal rows to Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS Notice 2024-29, and it is a jurisdictional gate rather than a judgement about Uruguayan law. Second, the register normalises those rows to a per-MASS figure carrying basis_class as_sold, while the regime they transcribe is expressed per volume of 4 percent acetic acid extract for fillable articles and per unit of food-contact surface area for flat and shallow ones, so binding them would publish a number in a basis the register row does not resolve. Third, they reach only the fillable (Category II) and over-three-litre and cooking-ware (Category III) configurations; no register row covers the Category I flat, shallow and lip-band configuration, which on a decorated plate or a drinking-vessel rim is the higher-release configuration and the one a ceiling would most need to govern. This build separately refuses to substitute the plastics specific migration limits for a glaze-release limit: the two are different extractions on different material families and the substitution would be a basis conflation. The cell is therefore a control with mandatory release testing and no invented number until 84/500/EEC as amended is ingested in its own EU rows and native bases. Aluminium is a structural constituent of every alumino-silicate glaze and body and of glass batches, so an aluminium release determination on this family measures the network itself; it is retained as a mandatory determination and no ceiling is invented for it. Ceramicware is the row for which the absent release regime is most consequential, so the control is written to be operative: every glaze and enamel colour is tested as its own lot, the lip band is tested separately, and a detection triggers escalation rather than a comparison against a borrowed number.
control.reference_method: Release testing on the filled or contact-surface article using 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid at the article's stated use temperature and duration (the release convention used for glazed, enamelled and glass food-contact articles), ICP-MS determination in the extract, with a separate determination on any decoration lying within 20 mm of the lip or on any interior decoration. Each result is reported in the native basis its article form generates and in no other: per dm2 of food-contact surface for a non-fillable or shallow article and for the decoration band within 20 mm of the lip, and per litre of extract (reportable as ug/kg on the stated 1 L = 1 kg convention) for a fillable article and for an article over three litres or intended for cooking. A per-dm2 result is never converted to a per-mass or per-volume result, and per-area and per-volume results are never pooled.

tableware-glassware.name: Glassware
tableware-glassware.native_basis: element release from the glaze, vitreous enamel or glass into food or food simulant, declared in TWO native bases: ug/dm2 of food-contact surface for non-fillable and shallow articles and for decoration within 20 mm of the lip (Directive 84/500/EEC Category I convention), and ug/L of 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid extract for fillable articles (Category II) and for articles over three litres and cooking ware (Category III), reportable as ug/kg only on the explicitly stated 1 L = 1 kg convention
tableware-glassware.native_basis_label: element RELEASE FROM THE GLAZE, VITREOUS ENAMEL OR GLASS NETWORK INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT, declared in TWO NATIVE BASES because the governing release regime is written in two and this row never merges them. BASIS A, for non-fillable and shallow articles and for any decoration lying within 20 mm of the lip: ug per dm2 of food-contact surface, the Directive 84/500/EEC Category I convention. BASIS B, for fillable articles (Category II) and for articles over three litres and cooking ware (Category III): ug per litre of 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid extract, reportable as ug/kg ONLY on the explicitly stated 1 L = 1 kg convention, which is the single unit conversion this row permits. CONVERSION OF A PER-AREA RESULT INTO A PER-MASS OR PER-VOLUME RESULT IS FORBIDDEN on this row: it requires a food-contact-area-per-kg-of-food assumption (the occurrence literature commonly uses 5 dm2 per kg of foodstuff) that this standard does not adopt, and adopting it would smuggle an unstated assumption into a certification number. Every result is reported in the basis its article form generates, and a per-dm2 result and a per-litre result are never pooled, averaged or compared. This is a RELEASE basis and not a total-content basis, and it is deliberately NOT the Reg (EU) 10/2011 plastics-simulant convention: a plastics specific migration limit is never substituted for a release limit on this family.
tableware-glassware.scope_note: Glass drinking and serving ware. The glass network is the food-contact surface. Two configurations raise the stakes: LEAD CRYSTAL, in which lead oxide is a bulk constituent of the glass at up to 24 percent or more and lead release into stored acidic beverages is documented, and applied EXTERIOR ENAMEL DECORATION, which is a hand-to-mouth and lip-contact pathway rather than a fill pathway. The release regime that governs both (EU 84/500/EEC for ceramic articles as the nearest instrument, the US FDA compliance-policy guide on lead in decorated glassware, and the Proposition 65 tableware judgments) is not present in the register as rows of its own jurisdiction; the only register rows carrying those numbers for this article class are four non-allowlisted Uruguayan rows, named and declined on stated grounds in every cell. The row is a control and the gap is recorded.
tableware-glassware.material: Soda-lime-silica tumblers, stemware and plates; lead crystal and crystal-glass stemware and decanters; opal and tempered glass; applied ceramic enamel decoration and painted exterior bands.
tableware-glassware.components: Sample and report separately: (1) interior glass surface, filled-article extraction; (2) lead-crystal articles as their own lot, with an extended-contact extraction representing a decanter or stored-beverage use case; (3) applied exterior enamel or painted decoration, and any decoration within 20 mm of the lip, tested by the lip-and-rim wipe and extraction convention rather than by fill extraction alone; (4) interior decoration or fill-line print; (5) any metal or plated stem, base or rim band.
tableware-glassware.audit_scope: food.contact|food contact|plastic food|utensil|cookware|cooking utensil|kitchen|tableware|crockery|ceramic|porcelain|earthenware|glaze|enamel|glassware|hollowware|packaging and containers|food-contact surface
tableware-glassware.basis_guard: element release|specific release|release into food|release into a food simulant|release into the food simulant|acetic acid|food-contact surface area|mg/dm2|per dm2
tableware-glassware.basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as element RELEASE from a glaze, vitreous-enamel or glass food-contact surface into food, a food simulant or the 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid extract convention, per dm2 of food-contact surface or per litre of extract, may anchor a cell on this row. The guard exists to reject the three foreign bases that surround this category and would otherwise look plausible: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents and not the article), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (CPSIA total lead in substrate, EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium percent-by-weight restrictions, RoHS homogeneous-material limits, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals), and the ARTICLE-EXTRACTION basis of the toy regime (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III and ASTM F963 soluble limits, which are element migration from scraped-off or coated TOY material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid, expressed per kg of MATERIAL, not per kg of food). Any of those would fail this guard and resolve to a gap rather than publish in the wrong basis. On this control row the guard is declaratory as well as operative: it records the only basis in which a future ingested instrument would be allowed to supply this row's numbers, so that a content limit, a food limit, a water limit or a plastics specific migration limit cannot later be dropped in as this row's release ceiling. The plastics clause is deliberately absent from this guard: a Reg (EU) 10/2011 value named here would fail the guard and resolve to a gap. DECLARED VACUOUS STATE (recorded, not overlooked): as written this guard matches ZERO live, non-draft and non-quarantined rows in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv, and that is its intended state. The release regime this row's basis family belongs to is not in the register in any form this row may bind, which is the same fact this row's control cells record and state in detail; a guard that admitted a live row today could only do so by admitting a foreign basis. The guard is nevertheless expressed in the register's own basis vocabulary (element or specific release, release into food or a food simulant, 4 percent acetic acid extract, per dm2 of food-contact surface, net device contribution to the treated water) so that a future correct ingest of that regime BINDS through it. The previous prose-sentence guard on this row would have REJECTED the very instruments it was waiting for and forced them to a gap, which is the defect this rewrite removes. Two limits on the guard's force are stated plainly rather than left implicit: the compiler returns on the control branch before basis resolution, so a guard is never evaluated on a control cell, and this note rather than the machine is what carries the guard's force on this row today. The engine change that would close that hole - an assertion that every declared basis_guard either matches at least one live register row or carries basis_guard_vacuous_by_design, failing the build otherwise - is recorded as a tooling gap and is outside this config's scope.

The regime that governs this material family in the real world is EU Council Directive 84/500/EEC as amended by Directive 2005/31/EC, supported in the United States by the FDA compliance-policy guides on lead in ceramicware and decorated glassware and by the California Proposition 65 tableware consent judgments; none of those instruments is present in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv as a row of its own jurisdiction, and each is recorded as a register gap for ingest through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway. What the register DOES hold for this exact article class is named here rather than passed over: four Uruguayan Reglamento Bromatologico Nacional section 12.5.13 rows carrying the same numbers as the EU Category II and Category III release values, namely uy_rbn_pb_ceramic_fillable_objects_4mgkg (lead, 4000 ug/kg) and uy_rbn_cd_ceramic_fillable_objects_0_3mgkg (cadmium, 300 ug/kg), both scoped to food-contact ceramic objects that can be filled, and uy_rbn_pb_cookware_storage_gt3l_1_5mgkg (lead, 1500 ug/kg) and uy_rbn_cd_cookware_storage_gt3l_0_1mgkg (cadmium, 100 ug/kg), both scoped to ceramic cooking utensils, packaging and storage containers with capacity over three litres. Those four rows are DECLINED on three stated grounds, and not because they are absent. First, Uruguay sits OUTSIDE the HMTc credible-regulator set used for anchoring in this build, so it cannot supply a published number without a recorded governance ruling; this is the same treatment already given on the metal rows to Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS Notice 2024-29, and it is a jurisdictional gate rather than a judgement about Uruguayan law. Second, the register normalises those rows to a per-MASS figure carrying basis_class as_sold, while the regime they transcribe is expressed per volume of 4 percent acetic acid extract for fillable articles and per unit of food-contact surface area for flat and shallow ones, so binding them would publish a number in a basis the register row does not resolve. Third, they reach only the fillable (Category II) and over-three-litre and cooking-ware (Category III) configurations; no register row covers the Category I flat, shallow and lip-band configuration, which on a decorated plate or a drinking-vessel rim is the higher-release configuration and the one a ceiling would most need to govern. This build separately refuses to substitute the plastics specific migration limits for a glaze-release limit: the two are different extractions on different material families and the substitution would be a basis conflation. The cell is therefore a control with mandatory release testing and no invented number until 84/500/EEC as amended is ingested in its own EU rows and native bases. Nickel occurs in glaze and enamel colourants (nickel oxide greys and browns) and in the ground-coat of vitreous enamel over steel. For glassware the two operative configurations are lead crystal, where lead is a bulk network constituent rather than a surface contaminant, and applied lip-adjacent decoration, where the exposure is lip contact rather than fill; both are tested as their own lots and neither is represented by a plain-tumbler result.
control.reference_method: Release testing on the filled or contact-surface article using 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid at the article's stated use temperature and duration (the release convention used for glazed, enamelled and glass food-contact articles), ICP-MS determination in the extract, with a separate determination on any decoration lying within 20 mm of the lip or on any interior decoration. Each result is reported in the native basis its article form generates and in no other: per dm2 of food-contact surface for a non-fillable or shallow article and for the decoration band within 20 mm of the lip, and per litre of extract (reportable as ug/kg on the stated 1 L = 1 kg convention) for a fillable article and for an article over three litres or intended for cooking. A per-dm2 result is never converted to a per-mass or per-volume result, and per-area and per-volume results are never pooled.
