tableware-metal-bottles-tumblers.name: Metal bottles/tumblers
tableware-metal-bottles-tumblers.native_basis: element release from the food-contact alloy into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
tableware-metal-bottles-tumblers.native_basis_label: element RELEASE FROM THE FOOD-CONTACT ALLOY INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT, µg/kg of food, determined against an acidic simulant at the article's stated use temperature and duration with the third successive release governing for repeat-use articles. This is a RELEASE basis on the food, not the plastics-simulant convention and not a total-content basis: the percent-by-weight lead limits on food-contact metals and solder are a separate MATERIAL-CONTENT obligation, disclosed as companions and never published here.
tableware-metal-bottles-tumblers.scope_note: Reusable metal drink containers. The food-contact surface is the interior alloy or its liner. The characteristic pathway is not the wall alloy but the BASE PLUG of a vacuum-insulated body, where a lead-bearing solder or braze seals the evacuation port and becomes an exposure route only if the covering cap detaches; that is the subject of well-known consumer-product recalls and Proposition 65 actions and is why the component plan requires the base to be tested and its cover retention verified as a mechanical requirement. No credible sovereign sets an element release ceiling for a metal food-contact article, so the row is a control; the Japanese and Korean percent-by-weight lead limits on food-contact metals and solder are disclosed as MATERIAL-CONTENT companions. TRACEABILITY OF THE COMPONENT POINTER: where this row's component plan refers a plastic component to "the plastics migration ceilings", that phrase resolves to a concrete published set of values inside this same standard and is not an unresolved pointer. It means the Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II values published on this category's plastics rows — eu_10_2011_pb_sml_nd (lead, not detectable at 10 ug/kg food), eu_10_2011_cd_sml_nd (cadmium, 2), eu_10_2011_tas_sml_nd (total arsenic, 10), eu_10_2011_thg_sml_nd (total mercury, 10), eu_10_2011_ni_sml (nickel, 20), eu_10_2011_al_sml (aluminium, 1000) and eu_10_2011_crtotal_sml_nd (total chromium, not detectable at 10), with tin excepted because the instrument lists no tin entry. Those values bind the plastic component as a SEPARATE obligation in its own material family and are never this row's published ceiling, which stays in this row's own native basis.
tableware-metal-bottles-tumblers.material: Single- and double-wall austenitic stainless steel and aluminium bottles and tumblers; interior lacquer or ceramic-coated liners on some aluminium bottles; vacuum-insulated bodies closed with a soldered or welded base plug; painted or powder-coated exteriors; plastic and silicone lids, straws and gaskets.
tableware-metal-bottles-tumblers.components: Sample and report separately: (1) interior wall alloy, acidic-simulant release at the highest claimed hold temperature and duration; (2) interior lacquer or ceramic liner where fitted, which is a coating and takes the polymeric or ceramic regime of its own family; (3) BASE PLUG solder or braze, analysed for lead content and tested for release with the cover removed, plus a cover-retention verification; (4) threaded neck, cut edges and any weld; (5) lid, gasket, straw and bite valve, bound by the plastics migration ceilings directly or by disclosed read-across; (6) exterior paint or powder coat, tested as a mouth-and-hand-contact surface at the lip.
tableware-metal-bottles-tumblers.audit_scope: food.contact|food contact|plastic food|utensil|cookware|cooking utensil|kitchen|tableware|crockery|ceramic|porcelain|earthenware|glaze|enamel|glassware|hollowware|packaging and containers|food-contact surface
tableware-metal-bottles-tumblers.basis_guard: element release|specific release|specific release limit|release into food|release into a food simulant|release into the food simulant|acetic acid
tableware-metal-bottles-tumblers.basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as element RELEASE from a metal or alloy food-contact surface into food or a food simulant may anchor a cell on this row. The guard exists to reject the three foreign bases that surround this category and would otherwise look plausible: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents and not the article), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (CPSIA total lead in substrate, EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium percent-by-weight restrictions, RoHS homogeneous-material limits, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals), and the ARTICLE-EXTRACTION basis of the toy regime (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III and ASTM F963 soluble limits, which are element migration from scraped-off or coated TOY material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid, expressed per kg of MATERIAL, not per kg of food). Any of those would fail this guard and resolve to a gap rather than publish in the wrong basis. On this control row the guard is declaratory as well as operative: it records the only basis in which a future ingested instrument would be allowed to supply this row's numbers, so that a content limit, a food limit, a water limit or a plastics specific migration limit cannot later be dropped in as this row's release ceiling. The plastics clause is deliberately absent from this guard: a Reg (EU) 10/2011 value named here would fail the guard and resolve to a gap. DECLARED VACUOUS STATE (recorded, not overlooked): as written this guard matches ZERO live, non-draft and non-quarantined rows in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv, and that is its intended state. The release regime this row's basis family belongs to is not in the register in any form this row may bind, which is the same fact this row's control cells record and state in detail; a guard that admitted a live row today could only do so by admitting a foreign basis. The guard is nevertheless expressed in the register's own basis vocabulary (element or specific release, release into food or a food simulant, 4 percent acetic acid extract, per dm2 of food-contact surface, net device contribution to the treated water) so that a future correct ingest of that regime BINDS through it. The previous prose-sentence guard on this row would have REJECTED the very instruments it was waiting for and forced them to a gap, which is the defect this rewrite removes. Two limits on the guard's force are stated plainly rather than left implicit: the compiler returns on the control branch before basis resolution, so a guard is never evaluated on a control cell, and this note rather than the machine is what carries the guard's force on this row today. The engine change that would close that hole - an assertion that every declared basis_guard either matches at least one live register row or carries basis_guard_vacuous_by_design, failing the build otherwise - is recorded as a tooling gap and is outside this config's scope.

control.rationale: No credible sovereign sets a numeric ceiling on element release from a metal or alloy food-contact article. Regulation (EU) 10/2011 governs plastics only; metals and alloys are a separate Regulation 1935/2004 Annex I material family for which the EU has adopted no specific measure, the US regulates food-contact substances without an element release ceiling, and Codex, FSANZ, Health Canada, the UK and Hong Kong set none. Testing is therefore mandatory on every certified lot with no invented ceiling: a limit borrowed from the plastics regulation would be a limit written for a different material family, and for an alloy surface the plastics nickel and aluminium values are not even achievable, so borrowing them would be an unfounded number rather than a stricter one. Lead in a food-contact metal article arrives from the alloy, from lead-bearing solder and brazing at joints and base plugs, and from plated or printed decoration on the interior. Japan Notice 370 (1959) and Korea MFDS Notice 2024-29 do set sovereign lead limits for food-contact metals, but they are percent-by-weight limits on the metal, solder and tin plating: a MATERIAL-CONTENT basis. Both jurisdictions also sit OUTSIDE the HMTc credible-regulator set used for anchoring in this build, so they could not supply a published number here even in the right basis; they are disclosed as real foreign obligations and must not be promoted to anchors without a recorded governance ruling. That obligation is disclosed as a companion and is verified on every certified article; it is not published as this row's release ceiling, because a content limit and a release limit are different measured quantities. On a vacuum-insulated bottle the binding component is the base-plug solder or braze, not the wall alloy; a wall-only result does not represent the article and is not accepted.
control.reference_method: Food-simulant release testing on each food-contact metal component under worst foreseeable use conditions (acidic simulant at the article's stated cooking or holding temperature and duration; for repeat-use articles the third successive release result governs), ICP-MS determination in the simulant, plus alloy-composition verification of every food-contact component by ICP-OES after acid digestion (XRF for screening only).

Testing is therefore mandatory on every certified lot with no invented ceiling: a limit borrowed from the plastics regulation would be a limit written for a different material family, and for an alloy surface the plastics nickel and aluminium values are not even achievable, so borrowing them would be an unfounded number rather than a stricter one. Tin release arrives from tinned linings, tinplate and tin-bearing solder. The sovereign tin numbers that exist are maximum levels on canned food, a FOOD basis on the contents rather than the article, and they are not published as this row's release ceiling. On a vacuum-insulated bottle the binding component is the base-plug solder or braze, not the wall alloy; a wall-only result does not represent the article and is not accepted.
control.reference_method: Food-simulant release testing on each food-contact metal component under worst foreseeable use conditions (acidic simulant at the article's stated cooking or holding temperature and duration; for repeat-use articles the third successive release result governs), ICP-MS determination in the simulant, plus alloy-composition verification of every food-contact component by ICP-OES after acid digestion (XRF for screening only).

tableware-plastic-drinkware.name: Plastic drinkware
tableware-plastic-drinkware.native_basis: specific element migration into food or food simulant (µg/kg food), Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II convention
tableware-plastic-drinkware.native_basis_label: specific element migration INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT from the polymeric food-contact surface, µg/kg of food, determined by the Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex III to V simulant, temperature and contact-time conventions. This is a MIGRATION basis and not a total-content basis: no cell on this row limits how much of an element the material CONTAINS, and no cell on this row is expressed per kg of material.
tableware-plastic-drinkware.scope_note: Plastic drinking vessels, directly within Reg (EU) 10/2011 as articles consisting exclusively of plastics. Repeat-use, so the third successive migration governs. Two configurations need naming: heavily PIGMENTED and printed ware, where lead chromate, cadmium sulfoselenide and chrome-green pigments are the element source, and MELAMINE and bamboo-melamine composite ware, which is a thermoset with filler and is the configuration most likely to fail on both element migration and hot-beverage contact conditions.
tableware-plastic-drinkware.material: Repeat-use polypropylene, Tritan copolyester, polycarbonate, SAN and melamine-formaldehyde tumblers, cups and picnic ware; printed and pigmented decoration; melamine and bamboo-melamine composite ware.
tableware-plastic-drinkware.components: Sample and report separately: (1) interior vessel surface at the third successive migration and at the highest claimed beverage temperature; (2) lip and rim band, including any decoration within 20 mm of the lip; (3) exterior print and pigment as a lip-and-hand-contact surface; (4) melamine or bamboo-composite formulations as their own lot; (5) lid, straw and valve components; (6) pigment masterbatch verification for lead chromate, cadmium pigment and chrome green.

tableware-plastic-drinkware.basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as specific element migration into food or a food simulant may anchor a cell on this row. The guard exists to reject the three foreign bases that surround this category and would otherwise look plausible: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents and not the article), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (CPSIA total lead in substrate, EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium percent-by-weight restrictions, RoHS homogeneous-material limits, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals), and the ARTICLE-EXTRACTION basis of the toy regime (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III and ASTM F963 soluble limits, which are element migration from scraped-off or coated TOY material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid, expressed per kg of MATERIAL, not per kg of food). Any of those would fail this guard and resolve to a gap rather than publish in the wrong basis.

Pb.label: Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II point 2: lead not detectable in the food or simulant, detection limit 0.01 mg/kg food
Pb.basis_label: specific element migration into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
Pb.substantiation: Lead is on the Annex II point 2 not-detectable list, so the published ceiling is the 0.01 mg/kg food detection limit and not a positive migration allowance. Plastic drinkware consists exclusively of plastics and is within this instrument's direct scope. This is a migration ceiling on the food or simulant and is never reported as a limit on the material's lead content; the material-content instruments (US CPSIA total lead in children's-product substrate, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS 2024-29 percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals and solder) are separate obligations in a different basis and are not this cell.

Cd.label: Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II point 2: cadmium not detectable in the food or simulant, detection limit 0.002 mg/kg food
Cd.basis_label: specific element migration into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
Cd.substantiation: Cadmium is on the Annex II point 2 not-detectable list; the published ceiling is the 0.002 mg/kg food detection limit, the strictest element value in the instrument. Plastic drinkware consists exclusively of plastics and is within this instrument's direct scope. The EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium restrictions on plastics, paints and recovered PVC are percent-by-weight content restrictions and are not read into this migration cell.

tAs.label: Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II point 2: arsenic (total element) not detectable in the food or simulant, detection limit 0.01 mg/kg food

Ni.basis_label: specific element migration into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
Ni.substantiation: Nickel carries a positive specific migration limit of 0.02 mg/kg food, the tightest positive SML in the Annex II element list. Plastic drinkware consists exclusively of plastics and is within this instrument's direct scope. This value governs the polymeric food-contact surface only; where a food-contact component of the article is a nickel-bearing alloy, that component sits in the alloy-release control regime described in this row's component plan, because the plastics SML was not written for and is not achievable by a bare stainless-steel surface.

control.rationale: Regulation (EU) 10/2011 Annex II lists no tin entry, and no credible sovereign sets a tin migration or release ceiling for a food-contact article of any material family. Tin is nonetheless a mandatory panel cell, because tin stabilisers in PVC compounds and tin-bearing solder are live pathways in parts of this category, so it is tested on every certified lot with no invented ceiling. This cell carries NO companion: the only sovereign tin numbers in existence are maximum levels on canned food, which are a FOOD basis on the contents of a tinplate container, and they are neither applicable to this row nor publishable as a migration ceiling. They are named as a companion only on the rows where a tinplate or crown component actually exists.
control.reference_method: EN 1186 / EN 13130 food-simulant migration testing on the finished article under its worst foreseeable use conditions (simulant, temperature and contact time selected per Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex III and Annex V; for repeat-use articles the third successive migration result governs), with ICP-MS determination of the element in the simulant.

Al.label: Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II point 1: aluminium specific migration limit 1 mg/kg food
Al.basis_label: specific element migration into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
Al.substantiation: Aluminium carries a positive specific migration limit of 1 mg/kg food, added by Reg (EU) 2016/1416. Plastic drinkware consists exclusively of plastics and is within this instrument's direct scope. This value governs the polymeric food-contact surface; it is not applied to an aluminium metal article, because an instrument written for plastics did not contemplate an article whose food-contact surface is the element itself.

Cr.label: Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II point 2: total chromium not detectable in the food or simulant, detection limit 0.01 mg/kg food; the 3.6 mg/kg food relaxation available on documented exclusion of chromium(VI) is declined
Cr.basis_label: specific element migration into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
Cr.substantiation: This total-chromium cell is deliberately published as a firm ceiling rather than the usual non-protective total-chromium screen, and the reason is structural to the instrument. Annex II point 2 as amended by Reg (EU) 2020/1245 sets total chromium at not detectable and permits a relaxed 3.6 mg/kg food limit only where the operator documents that chromium(VI) is absent. The non-detect branch therefore exists precisely because hexavalent chromium cannot be assumed absent, which makes it the hexavalent-chromium-conservative form of the requirement rather than a chromium(III)-dominated artefact. HMTc publishes the non-detect branch and declines the relaxation, and the hexavalent-chromium cell is bounded by this value. Plastic drinkware consists exclusively of plastics and is within this instrument's direct scope.

tableware-decorative-decals-coatings.name: Decorative decals/coatings on tableware
tableware-decorative-decals-coatings.native_basis: element release from the glaze, vitreous enamel or glass into food or food simulant, declared in TWO native bases: ug/dm2 of food-contact surface for non-fillable and shallow articles and for decoration within 20 mm of the lip (Directive 84/500/EEC Category I convention), and ug/L of 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid extract for fillable articles (Category II) and for articles over three litres and cooking ware (Category III), reportable as ug/kg only on the explicitly stated 1 L = 1 kg convention
tableware-decorative-decals-coatings.native_basis_label: element RELEASE FROM THE GLAZE, VITREOUS ENAMEL OR GLASS NETWORK INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT, declared in TWO NATIVE BASES because the governing release regime is written in two and this row never merges them. BASIS A, for non-fillable and shallow articles and for any decoration lying within 20 mm of the lip: ug per dm2 of food-contact surface, the Directive 84/500/EEC Category I convention. BASIS B, for fillable articles (Category II) and for articles over three litres and cooking ware (Category III): ug per litre of 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid extract, reportable as ug/kg ONLY on the explicitly stated 1 L = 1 kg convention, which is the single unit conversion this row permits. CONVERSION OF A PER-AREA RESULT INTO A PER-MASS OR PER-VOLUME RESULT IS FORBIDDEN on this row: it requires a food-contact-area-per-kg-of-food assumption (the occurrence literature commonly uses 5 dm2 per kg of foodstuff) that this standard does not adopt, and adopting it would smuggle an unstated assumption into a certification number. Every result is reported in the basis its article form generates, and a per-dm2 result and a per-litre result are never pooled, averaged or compared. This is a RELEASE basis and not a total-content basis, and it is deliberately NOT the Reg (EU) 10/2011 plastics-simulant convention: a plastics specific migration limit is never substituted for a release limit on this family.
tableware-decorative-decals-coatings.scope_note: The decoration itself, considered separately from the article it is applied to, because decoration is a distinct release surface with a distinct exposure route. Decoration that lies on an interior surface is a fill-contact pathway. Decoration within 20 mm of the lip is a LIP-CONTACT pathway, and decoration on the exterior body is a HAND-TO-MOUTH pathway; none of the three is represented by a fill extraction on an undecorated area. The applicable lead-and-cadmium release regime for applied decoration on tableware (EU 84/500/EEC and its amendments, the FDA compliance-policy guides on ceramicware and decorated glassware, and the Proposition 65 tableware consent judgments) is not present in the register as rows of its own jurisdiction; the only register rows carrying those numbers for this article class are four non-allowlisted Uruguayan rows, named and declined on stated grounds in every cell. The row is a control and the gap is recorded.
tableware-decorative-decals-coatings.material: On-glaze and in-glaze ceramic enamel decals and transfers; organic overprint and lustre; applied vitreous enamel bands; gold and platinum lustre; painted and powder-coated exterior surfaces on drinkware.
tableware-decorative-decals-coatings.components: Sample and report separately: (1) each decal, enamel and lustre colour as its own lot, since release is colour-specific; (2) decoration on interior surfaces, by fill extraction; (3) decoration within 20 mm of the lip, by the lip-and-rim convention; (4) exterior body decoration, by a hand-contact wipe and extraction; (5) gold and platinum lustre and any metallic band, which additionally carry an alloy-impurity route; (6) decoration after the declared number of dishwasher cycles, because abraded and etched enamel releases more than as-supplied enamel.

tableware-decorative-decals-coatings.basis_guard: element release|specific release|release into food|release into a food simulant|release into the food simulant|acetic acid|food-contact surface area|mg/dm2|per dm2
tableware-decorative-decals-coatings.basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as element RELEASE from a glaze, vitreous-enamel or glass food-contact surface into food, a food simulant or the 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid extract convention, per dm2 of food-contact surface or per litre of extract, may anchor a cell on this row. The guard exists to reject the three foreign bases that surround this category and would otherwise look plausible: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents and not the article), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (CPSIA total lead in substrate, EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium percent-by-weight restrictions, RoHS homogeneous-material limits, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals), and the ARTICLE-EXTRACTION basis of the toy regime (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III and ASTM F963 soluble limits, which are element migration from scraped-off or coated TOY material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid, expressed per kg of MATERIAL, not per kg of food). Any of those would fail this guard and resolve to a gap rather than publish in the wrong basis. On this control row the guard is declaratory as well as operative: it records the only basis in which a future ingested instrument would be allowed to supply this row's numbers, so that a content limit, a food limit, a water limit or a plastics specific migration limit cannot later be dropped in as this row's release ceiling. The plastics clause is deliberately absent from this guard: a Reg (EU) 10/2011 value named here would fail the guard and resolve to a gap. DECLARED VACUOUS STATE (recorded, not overlooked): as written this guard matches ZERO live, non-draft and non-quarantined rows in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv, and that is its intended state. The release regime this row's basis family belongs to is not in the register in any form this row may bind, which is the same fact this row's control cells record and state in detail; a guard that admitted a live row today could only do so by admitting a foreign basis. The guard is nevertheless expressed in the register's own basis vocabulary (element or specific release, release into food or a food simulant, 4 percent acetic acid extract, per dm2 of food-contact surface, net device contribution to the treated water) so that a future correct ingest of that regime BINDS through it. The previous prose-sentence guard on this row would have REJECTED the very instruments it was waiting for and forced them to a gap, which is the defect this rewrite removes. Two limits on the guard's force are stated plainly rather than left implicit: the compiler returns on the control branch before basis resolution, so a guard is never evaluated on a control cell, and this note rather than the machine is what carries the guard's force on this row today. The engine change that would close that hole - an assertion that every declared basis_guard either matches at least one live register row or carries basis_guard_vacuous_by_design, failing the build otherwise - is recorded as a tooling gap and is outside this config's scope.

control.rationale: No credible sovereign release ceiling for this material family is available to anchor this cell, and the register position is stated exactly rather than by assertion of absence. The regime that governs this material family in the real world is EU Council Directive 84/500/EEC as amended by Directive 2005/31/EC, supported in the United States by the FDA compliance-policy guides on lead in ceramicware and decorated glassware and by the California Proposition 65 tableware consent judgments; none of those instruments is present in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv as a row of its own jurisdiction, and each is recorded as a register gap for ingest through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway. What the register DOES hold for this exact article class is named here rather than passed over: four Uruguayan Reglamento Bromatologico Nacional section 12.5.13 rows carrying the same numbers as the EU Category II and Category III release values, namely uy_rbn_pb_ceramic_fillable_objects_4mgkg (lead, 4000 ug/kg) and uy_rbn_cd_ceramic_fillable_objects_0_3mgkg (cadmium, 300 ug/kg), both scoped to food-contact ceramic objects that can be filled, and uy_rbn_pb_cookware_storage_gt3l_1_5mgkg (lead, 1500 ug/kg) and uy_rbn_cd_cookware_storage_gt3l_0_1mgkg (cadmium, 100 ug/kg), both scoped to ceramic cooking utensils, packaging and storage containers with capacity over three litres. Those four rows are DECLINED on three stated grounds, and not because they are absent. First, Uruguay sits OUTSIDE the HMTc credible-regulator set used for anchoring in this build, so it cannot supply a published number without a recorded governance ruling; this is the same treatment already given on the metal rows to Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS Notice 2024-29, and it is a jurisdictional gate rather than a judgement about Uruguayan law. Second, the register normalises those rows to a per-MASS figure carrying basis_class as_sold, while the regime they transcribe is expressed per volume of 4 percent acetic acid extract for fillable articles and per unit of food-contact surface area for flat and shallow ones, so binding them would publish a number in a basis the register row does not resolve. Third, they reach only the fillable (Category II) and over-three-litre and cooking-ware (Category III) configurations; no register row covers the Category I flat, shallow and lip-band configuration, which on a decorated plate or a drinking-vessel rim is the higher-release configuration and the one a ceiling would most need to govern. This build separately refuses to substitute the plastics specific migration limits for a glaze-release limit: the two are different extractions on different material families and the substitution would be a basis conflation. The cell is therefore a control with mandatory release testing and no invented number until 84/500/EEC as amended is ingested in its own EU rows and native bases. Lead is the dominant pathway for this material family: lead-fluxed and lead-bisilicate glazes, lead-bearing on-glaze enamels and applied decoration, and under-fired or acid-attacked glaze surfaces all release lead into acidic food. It is the single cell where the absent release regime matters most, and the gap is recorded rather than papered over with a plastics value. This row's unit of test is the decoration colour, not the article: each colour is a separate lot, and the three exposure routes (fill, lip and hand-to-mouth) are reported separately rather than pooled.
control.reference_method: Release testing on the filled or contact-surface article using 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid at the article's stated use temperature and duration (the release convention used for glazed, enamelled and glass food-contact articles), ICP-MS determination in the extract, with a separate determination on any decoration lying within 20 mm of the lip or on any interior decoration. Each result is reported in the native basis its article form generates and in no other: per dm2 of food-contact surface for a non-fillable or shallow article and for the decoration band within 20 mm of the lip, and per litre of extract (reportable as ug/kg on the stated 1 L = 1 kg convention) for a fillable article and for an article over three litres or intended for cooking. A per-dm2 result is never converted to a per-mass or per-volume result, and per-area and per-volume results are never pooled.

cookware-metal-alloy.name: Metal and alloy cookware (cast iron, stainless steel, aluminum)
cookware-metal-alloy.native_basis: element release from the food-contact alloy into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
cookware-metal-alloy.native_basis_label: element RELEASE FROM THE FOOD-CONTACT ALLOY INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT, µg/kg of food, determined against an acidic simulant at the article's stated use temperature and duration with the third successive release governing for repeat-use articles. This is a RELEASE basis on the food, not the plastics-simulant convention and not a total-content basis: the percent-by-weight lead limits on food-contact metals and solder are a separate MATERIAL-CONTENT obligation, disclosed as companions and never published here.
cookware-metal-alloy.scope_note: Cookware whose food-contact surface is bare metal or alloy. This is the alloy-leach pathway in its pure form: nickel and chromium release from austenitic stainless steel and aluminium release from bare and anodised aluminium into acidic, saline and long-simmered food are documented and material, and they are exactly the pathways for which no credible sovereign has set a release ceiling. The row is therefore a control across the panel, with mandatory release testing at the article's stated cooking conditions and alloy verification on every food-contact component. The Japanese and Korean percent-by-weight lead limits on food-contact metals and solder are disclosed as MATERIAL-CONTENT companions and verified as a separate obligation.
cookware-metal-alloy.material: Bare and seasoned cast iron; austenitic stainless steel, including clad and tri-ply constructions with an aluminium or copper core; bare, anodised and spun aluminium; carbon-steel woks; riveted or welded handle attachments.
cookware-metal-alloy.components: Sample and report separately: (1) interior cooking surface alloy, acidic-simulant release at the stated maximum cooking temperature and duration, third successive release governing; (2) rivets and their heads on the interior surface, which are frequently a different alloy from the body; (3) welds, brazes and any solder; (4) exposed core layer at a cut or ground rim on clad construction; (5) anodised layer integrity and the release result after the declared abrasion conditioning; (6) seasoning or factory pre-seasoning layer on cast iron and carbon steel.
cookware-metal-alloy.audit_scope: food.contact|food contact|plastic food|utensil|cookware|cooking utensil|kitchen|tableware|crockery|ceramic|porcelain|earthenware|glaze|enamel|glassware|hollowware|packaging and containers|food-contact surface
cookware-metal-alloy.basis_guard: element release|specific release|specific release limit|release into food|release into a food simulant|release into the food simulant|acetic acid
cookware-metal-alloy.basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as element RELEASE from a metal or alloy food-contact surface into food or a food simulant may anchor a cell on this row. The guard exists to reject the three foreign bases that surround this category and would otherwise look plausible: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents and not the article), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (CPSIA total lead in substrate, EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium percent-by-weight restrictions, RoHS homogeneous-material limits, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals), and the ARTICLE-EXTRACTION basis of the toy regime (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III and ASTM F963 soluble limits, which are element migration from scraped-off or coated TOY material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid, expressed per kg of MATERIAL, not per kg of food). Any of those would fail this guard and resolve to a gap rather than publish in the wrong basis. On this control row the guard is declaratory as well as operative: it records the only basis in which a future ingested instrument would be allowed to supply this row's numbers, so that a content limit, a food limit, a water limit or a plastics specific migration limit cannot later be dropped in as this row's release ceiling. The plastics clause is deliberately absent from this guard: a Reg (EU) 10/2011 value named here would fail the guard and resolve to a gap. DECLARED VACUOUS STATE (recorded, not overlooked): as written this guard matches ZERO live, non-draft and non-quarantined rows in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv, and that is its intended state. The release regime this row's basis family belongs to is not in the register in any form this row may bind, which is the same fact this row's control cells record and state in detail; a guard that admitted a live row today could only do so by admitting a foreign basis. The guard is nevertheless expressed in the register's own basis vocabulary (element or specific release, release into food or a food simulant, 4 percent acetic acid extract, per dm2 of food-contact surface, net device contribution to the treated water) so that a future correct ingest of that regime BINDS through it. The previous prose-sentence guard on this row would have REJECTED the very instruments it was waiting for and forced them to a gap, which is the defect this rewrite removes. Two limits on the guard's force are stated plainly rather than left implicit: the compiler returns on the control branch before basis resolution, so a guard is never evaluated on a control cell, and this note rather than the machine is what carries the guard's force on this row today. The engine change that would close that hole - an assertion that every declared basis_guard either matches at least one live register row or carries basis_guard_vacuous_by_design, failing the build otherwise - is recorded as a tooling gap and is outside this config's scope.

control.rationale: No credible sovereign sets a numeric ceiling on element release from a metal or alloy food-contact article. Regulation (EU) 10/2011 governs plastics only; metals and alloys are a separate Regulation 1935/2004 Annex I material family for which the EU has adopted no specific measure, the US regulates food-contact substances without an element release ceiling, and Codex, FSANZ, Health Canada, the UK and Hong Kong set none. Testing is therefore mandatory on every certified lot with no invented ceiling: a limit borrowed from the plastics regulation would be a limit written for a different material family, and for an alloy surface the plastics nickel and aluminium values are not even achievable, so borrowing them would be an unfounded number rather than a stricter one. Lead in a food-contact metal article arrives from the alloy, from lead-bearing solder and brazing at joints and base plugs, and from plated or printed decoration on the interior. Japan Notice 370 (1959) and Korea MFDS Notice 2024-29 do set sovereign lead limits for food-contact metals, but they are percent-by-weight limits on the metal, solder and tin plating: a MATERIAL-CONTENT basis. Both jurisdictions also sit OUTSIDE the HMTc credible-regulator set used for anchoring in this build, so they could not supply a published number here even in the right basis; they are disclosed as real foreign obligations and must not be promoted to anchors without a recorded governance ruling. That obligation is disclosed as a companion and is verified on every certified article; it is not published as this row's release ceiling, because a content limit and a release limit are different measured quantities. Nickel and aluminium are the operative cells on this row and are the reason it cannot borrow the plastics values: a bare austenitic stainless surface does not meet 0.02 mg/kg food nickel and a bare aluminium surface does not meet 1 mg/kg food aluminium, so importing those numbers would publish an unfounded ceiling rather than a strict one.
control.reference_method: Food-simulant release testing on each food-contact metal component under worst foreseeable use conditions (acidic simulant at the article's stated cooking or holding temperature and duration; for repeat-use articles the third successive release result governs), ICP-MS determination in the simulant, plus alloy-composition verification of every food-contact component by ICP-OES after acid digestion (XRF for screening only).

cookware-nonstick-coated.name: Nonstick-coated cookware
cookware-nonstick-coated.native_basis: specific element migration into food or food simulant (µg/kg food), Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II convention
cookware-nonstick-coated.native_basis_label: specific element migration INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT from the polymeric food-contact surface, µg/kg of food, determined by the Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex III to V simulant, temperature and contact-time conventions. This is a MIGRATION basis and not a total-content basis: no cell on this row limits how much of an element the material CONTAINS, and no cell on this row is expressed per kg of material.
cookware-nonstick-coated.scope_note: Cookware whose food-contact surface is a cured fluoropolymer coating. Coatings are a Regulation 1935/2004 Annex I material family for which the EU has adopted no specific measure, so the exact cell is unregulated and the published ceilings are a disclosed read-across from the plastics instrument, which is the nearest applicable sovereign value in the identical basis and is itself a fluoropolymer-compatible regime. The ceilings apply to the article as placed on market AND after the declared abrasion and thermal conditioning, because the certification question for a coated pan is whether the coating still isolates the substrate after realistic use; a pristine-coating result alone does not represent the article. Exposed interior rivets and any breached area are metal food-contact surfaces and fall to the alloy-release control regime under the component plan. This row is scoped to the ELEMENT panel; per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances are a separate and larger question that this standard does not address and does not imply anything about.
cookware-nonstick-coated.material: Fluoropolymer (PTFE and PTFE-copolymer) coating systems, usually primer plus midcoat plus topcoat, applied to spun or forged aluminium or to stainless steel; exposed stainless rivets on the interior; some reinforced with ceramic or mineral particles.
cookware-nonstick-coated.components: Sample and report separately: (1) intact coating on the cooking surface, before and after the declared abrasion and thermal-cycling conditioning; (2) exposed stainless or aluminium rivets on the interior, under the alloy-release regime; (3) deliberately scored or abraded coating representing end-of-life, to expose the substrate contribution; (4) exposed substrate at the rim and any cut edge; (5) coating pigment and any ceramic or mineral reinforcement; (6) primer layer, tested where the topcoat is thin enough not to constitute a functional barrier.
cookware-nonstick-coated.audit_scope: food.contact|food contact|plastic food|utensil|cookware|cooking utensil|kitchen|tableware|crockery|ceramic|porcelain|earthenware|glaze|enamel|glassware|hollowware|packaging and containers|food-contact surface
cookware-nonstick-coated.basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as specific element migration into food or a food simulant may anchor a cell on this row. The guard exists to reject the three foreign bases that surround this category and would otherwise look plausible: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents and not the article), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (CPSIA total lead in substrate, EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium percent-by-weight restrictions, RoHS homogeneous-material limits, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals), and the ARTICLE-EXTRACTION basis of the toy regime (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III and ASTM F963 soluble limits, which are element migration from scraped-off or coated TOY material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid, expressed per kg of MATERIAL, not per kg of food). Any of those would fail this guard and resolve to a gap rather than publish in the wrong basis.

read_across.label: read-across of the EU 10/2011 Annex II point 2 lead non-detect requirement (0.01 mg/kg food)
read_across.substantiation: The exact cell is unregulated: the food-contact surface is a cured liquid-applied coating, and coatings and varnishes are a Regulation 1935/2004 Annex I material family for which the EU has adopted no specific measure, while Reg (EU) 10/2011 reaches plastic layers in multi-material multi-layer articles but was not written for a sprayed and stoved coating system. cookware-ceramic-coated.name: Ceramic-coated cookware
cookware-ceramic-coated.native_basis: element release from the glaze, vitreous enamel or glass into food or food simulant, declared in TWO native bases: ug/dm2 of food-contact surface for non-fillable and shallow articles and for decoration within 20 mm of the lip (Directive 84/500/EEC Category I convention), and ug/L of 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid extract for fillable articles (Category II) and for articles over three litres and cooking ware (Category III), reportable as ug/kg only on the explicitly stated 1 L = 1 kg convention
cookware-ceramic-coated.native_basis_label: element RELEASE FROM THE GLAZE, VITREOUS ENAMEL OR GLASS NETWORK INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT, declared in TWO NATIVE BASES because the governing release regime is written in two and this row never merges them. BASIS A, for non-fillable and shallow articles and for any decoration lying within 20 mm of the lip: ug per dm2 of food-contact surface, the Directive 84/500/EEC Category I convention. BASIS B, for fillable articles (Category II) and for articles over three litres and cooking ware (Category III): ug per litre of 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid extract, reportable as ug/kg ONLY on the explicitly stated 1 L = 1 kg convention, which is the single unit conversion this row permits. CONVERSION OF A PER-AREA RESULT INTO A PER-MASS OR PER-VOLUME RESULT IS FORBIDDEN on this row: it requires a food-contact-area-per-kg-of-food assumption (the occurrence literature commonly uses 5 dm2 per kg of foodstuff) that this standard does not adopt, and adopting it would smuggle an unstated assumption into a certification number. Every result is reported in the basis its article form generates, and a per-dm2 result and a per-litre result are never pooled, averaged or compared. This is a RELEASE basis and not a total-content basis, and it is deliberately NOT the Reg (EU) 10/2011 plastics-simulant convention: a plastics specific migration limit is never substituted for a release limit on this family.
cookware-ceramic-coated.scope_note: Cookware whose food-contact surface is an INORGANIC coating: a sol-gel or vitreous enamel layer rather than a polymer. That places the row in the glaze-and-enamel release family, not the plastics family, and the applicable lead-and-cadmium release regime for that family (EU 84/500/EEC and its amendments, whose Art. 1(2) reaches vitreous-enamelled articles, and the FDA compliance-policy guide route) is not present in the register as rows of its own jurisdiction; the only register rows carrying those numbers for this article class are four non-allowlisted Uruguayan rows, named and declined on stated grounds in every cell. The row is therefore a control and the gap is recorded; the plastics migration limits are not substituted, because a fired inorganic coating and a polymer film are different material families extracted by different methods. Coloured enamel interiors are the configuration of concern, since frit colourants are the element source.
cookware-ceramic-coated.material: Sol-gel silica and silicone-hybrid inorganic coating systems on aluminium; true vitreous-enamel-on-steel and enamel-on-cast-iron cookware; enamelled interiors and exteriors with coloured frit.

cookware-ceramic-coated.basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as element RELEASE from a glaze, vitreous-enamel or glass food-contact surface into food, a food simulant or the 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid extract convention, per dm2 of food-contact surface or per litre of extract, may anchor a cell on this row. The guard exists to reject the three foreign bases that surround this category and would otherwise look plausible: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents and not the article), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (CPSIA total lead in substrate, EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium percent-by-weight restrictions, RoHS homogeneous-material limits, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals), and the ARTICLE-EXTRACTION basis of the toy regime (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III and ASTM F963 soluble limits, which are element migration from scraped-off or coated TOY material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid, expressed per kg of MATERIAL, not per kg of food). Any of those would fail this guard and resolve to a gap rather than publish in the wrong basis. On this control row the guard is declaratory as well as operative: it records the only basis in which a future ingested instrument would be allowed to supply this row's numbers, so that a content limit, a food limit, a water limit or a plastics specific migration limit cannot later be dropped in as this row's release ceiling. The plastics clause is deliberately absent from this guard: a Reg (EU) 10/2011 value named here would fail the guard and resolve to a gap. DECLARED VACUOUS STATE (recorded, not overlooked): as written this guard matches ZERO live, non-draft and non-quarantined rows in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv, and that is its intended state. The release regime this row's basis family belongs to is not in the register in any form this row may bind, which is the same fact this row's control cells record and state in detail; a guard that admitted a live row today could only do so by admitting a foreign basis. The guard is nevertheless expressed in the register's own basis vocabulary (element or specific release, release into food or a food simulant, 4 percent acetic acid extract, per dm2 of food-contact surface, net device contribution to the treated water) so that a future correct ingest of that regime BINDS through it. The previous prose-sentence guard on this row would have REJECTED the very instruments it was waiting for and forced them to a gap, which is the defect this rewrite removes. Two limits on the guard's force are stated plainly rather than left implicit: the compiler returns on the control branch before basis resolution, so a guard is never evaluated on a control cell, and this note rather than the machine is what carries the guard's force on this row today. The engine change that would close that hole - an assertion that every declared basis_guard either matches at least one live register row or carries basis_guard_vacuous_by_design, failing the build otherwise - is recorded as a tooling gap and is outside this config's scope.

control.rationale: No credible sovereign release ceiling for this material family is available to anchor this cell, and the register position is stated exactly rather than by assertion of absence. The regime that governs this material family in the real world is EU Council Directive 84/500/EEC as amended by Directive 2005/31/EC, supported in the United States by the FDA compliance-policy guides on lead in ceramicware and decorated glassware and by the California Proposition 65 tableware consent judgments; none of those instruments is present in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv as a row of its own jurisdiction, and each is recorded as a register gap for ingest through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway. What the register DOES hold for this exact article class is named here rather than passed over: four Uruguayan Reglamento Bromatologico Nacional section 12.5.13 rows carrying the same numbers as the EU Category II and Category III release values, namely uy_rbn_pb_ceramic_fillable_objects_4mgkg (lead, 4000 ug/kg) and uy_rbn_cd_ceramic_fillable_objects_0_3mgkg (cadmium, 300 ug/kg), both scoped to food-contact ceramic objects that can be filled, and uy_rbn_pb_cookware_storage_gt3l_1_5mgkg (lead, 1500 ug/kg) and uy_rbn_cd_cookware_storage_gt3l_0_1mgkg (cadmium, 100 ug/kg), both scoped to ceramic cooking utensils, packaging and storage containers with capacity over three litres. Those four rows are DECLINED on three stated grounds, and not because they are absent. First, Uruguay sits OUTSIDE the HMTc credible-regulator set used for anchoring in this build, so it cannot supply a published number without a recorded governance ruling; this is the same treatment already given on the metal rows to Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS Notice 2024-29, and it is a jurisdictional gate rather than a judgement about Uruguayan law. Second, the register normalises those rows to a per-MASS figure carrying basis_class as_sold, while the regime they transcribe is expressed per volume of 4 percent acetic acid extract for fillable articles and per unit of food-contact surface area for flat and shallow ones, so binding them would publish a number in a basis the register row does not resolve. Third, they reach only the fillable (Category II) and over-three-litre and cooking-ware (Category III) configurations; no register row covers the Category I flat, shallow and lip-band configuration, which on a decorated plate or a drinking-vessel rim is the higher-release configuration and the one a ceiling would most need to govern. This build separately refuses to substitute the plastics specific migration limits for a glaze-release limit: the two are different extractions on different material families and the substitution would be a basis conflation. The cell is therefore a control with mandatory release testing and no invented number until 84/500/EEC as amended is ingested in its own EU rows and native bases. Lead is the dominant pathway for this material family: lead-fluxed and lead-bisilicate glazes, lead-bearing on-glaze enamels and applied decoration, and under-fired or acid-attacked glaze surfaces all release lead into acidic food. It is the single cell where the absent release regime matters most, and the gap is recorded rather than papered over with a plastics value. Ceramic-coated and enamelled cookware sits in the glaze-release family rather than the plastics family, so it inherits this family's absent regime; coloured interior enamel is tested colour by colour and after abrasion and thermal-shock conditioning.
control.reference_method: Release testing on the filled or contact-surface article using 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid at the article's stated use temperature and duration (the release convention used for glazed, enamelled and glass food-contact articles), ICP-MS determination in the extract, with a separate determination on any decoration lying within 20 mm of the lip or on any interior decoration. Each result is reported in the native basis its article form generates and in no other: per dm2 of food-contact surface for a non-fillable or shallow article and for the decoration band within 20 mm of the lip, and per litre of extract (reportable as ug/kg on the stated 1 L = 1 kg convention) for a fillable article and for an article over three litres or intended for cooking. A per-dm2 result is never converted to a per-mass or per-volume result, and per-area and per-volume results are never pooled.

control.rationale: No credible sovereign sets a numeric ceiling on element release from a metal or alloy food-contact article. Regulation (EU) 10/2011 governs plastics only; metals and alloys are a separate Regulation 1935/2004 Annex I material family for which the EU has adopted no specific measure, the US regulates food-contact substances without an element release ceiling, and Codex, FSANZ, Health Canada, the UK and Hong Kong set none. Testing is therefore mandatory on every certified lot with no invented ceiling: a limit borrowed from the plastics regulation would be a limit written for a different material family, and for an alloy surface the plastics nickel and aluminium values are not even achievable, so borrowing them would be an unfounded number rather than a stricter one. Lead in a food-contact metal article arrives from the alloy, from lead-bearing solder and brazing at joints and base plugs, and from plated or printed decoration on the interior. Japan Notice 370 (1959) and Korea MFDS Notice 2024-29 do set sovereign lead limits for food-contact metals, but they are percent-by-weight limits on the metal, solder and tin plating: a MATERIAL-CONTENT basis. Both jurisdictions also sit OUTSIDE the HMTc credible-regulator set used for anchoring in this build, so they could not supply a published number here even in the right basis; they are disclosed as real foreign obligations and must not be promoted to anchors without a recorded governance ruling. That obligation is disclosed as a companion and is verified on every certified article; it is not published as this row's release ceiling, because a content limit and a release limit are different measured quantities. Bakeware release testing must be run at the stated baking temperature and duration rather than only at the ambient acidic-simulant convention, because dry high-temperature contact is this row's actual use condition.
control.reference_method: Food-simulant release testing on each food-contact metal component under worst foreseeable use conditions (acidic simulant at the article's stated cooking or holding temperature and duration; for repeat-use articles the third successive release result governs), ICP-MS determination in the simulant, plus alloy-composition verification of every food-contact component by ICP-OES after acid digestion (XRF for screening only).

utensils-metal.name: Metal utensils
utensils-metal.native_basis: element release from the food-contact alloy into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
utensils-metal.native_basis_label: element RELEASE FROM THE FOOD-CONTACT ALLOY INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT, µg/kg of food, determined against an acidic simulant at the article's stated use temperature and duration with the third successive release governing for repeat-use articles. This is a RELEASE basis on the food, not the plastics-simulant convention and not a total-content basis: the percent-by-weight lead limits on food-contact metals and solder are a separate MATERIAL-CONTENT obligation, disclosed as companions and never published here.
utensils-metal.scope_note: Metal utensils and flatware, whose food-contact surface is bare or plated alloy, so the row takes the metal-article release control regime. Contact is short but repeated and includes MOUTH CONTACT, which flatware shares with drinkware and which the component plan treats as its own exposure route. Hollow-handle flatware is called out because the handle-to-bowl joint is filled with cement or solder and is a documented lead route on legacy and low-cost stock. Plated utensils are tested intact and at worn areas, since plating wear exposes a different substrate alloy.
utensils-metal.material: Austenitic and ferritic stainless-steel flatware, serving and cooking utensils; plated flatware (silver-plated, nickel-plated, gold-plated, titanium-nitride coated); aluminium and cast-alloy utensils; brass and bronze serving pieces; hollow-handle flatware with a solder or resin-filled joint.
utensils-metal.components: Sample and report separately: (1) bowl, tine and blade food-contact surface, acidic-simulant release; (2) mouth-contact surface, by the lip-and-mouth convention rather than fill extraction; (3) HOLLOW-HANDLE joint filler and any solder, analysed for lead content and tested for release; (4) plating, intact and at worn or flaked areas, with substrate alloy identified; (5) decorative applied colour, enamel or lacquer on a handle within mouth-contact reach; (6) brass and bronze serving pieces as their own lot.
utensils-metal.audit_scope: food.contact|food contact|plastic food|utensil|cookware|cooking utensil|kitchen|tableware|crockery|ceramic|porcelain|earthenware|glaze|enamel|glassware|hollowware|packaging and containers|food-contact surface
utensils-metal.basis_guard: element release|specific release|specific release limit|release into food|release into a food simulant|release into the food simulant|acetic acid
utensils-metal.basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as element RELEASE from a metal or alloy food-contact surface into food or a food simulant may anchor a cell on this row. The guard exists to reject the three foreign bases that surround this category and would otherwise look plausible: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents and not the article), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (CPSIA total lead in substrate, EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium percent-by-weight restrictions, RoHS homogeneous-material limits, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals), and the ARTICLE-EXTRACTION basis of the toy regime (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III and ASTM F963 soluble limits, which are element migration from scraped-off or coated TOY material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid, expressed per kg of MATERIAL, not per kg of food). Any of those would fail this guard and resolve to a gap rather than publish in the wrong basis. On this control row the guard is declaratory as well as operative: it records the only basis in which a future ingested instrument would be allowed to supply this row's numbers, so that a content limit, a food limit, a water limit or a plastics specific migration limit cannot later be dropped in as this row's release ceiling. The plastics clause is deliberately absent from this guard: a Reg (EU) 10/2011 value named here would fail the guard and resolve to a gap. DECLARED VACUOUS STATE (recorded, not overlooked): as written this guard matches ZERO live, non-draft and non-quarantined rows in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv, and that is its intended state. The release regime this row's basis family belongs to is not in the register in any form this row may bind, which is the same fact this row's control cells record and state in detail; a guard that admitted a live row today could only do so by admitting a foreign basis. The guard is nevertheless expressed in the register's own basis vocabulary (element or specific release, release into food or a food simulant, 4 percent acetic acid extract, per dm2 of food-contact surface, net device contribution to the treated water) so that a future correct ingest of that regime BINDS through it. The previous prose-sentence guard on this row would have REJECTED the very instruments it was waiting for and forced them to a gap, which is the defect this rewrite removes. Two limits on the guard's force are stated plainly rather than left implicit: the compiler returns on the control branch before basis resolution, so a guard is never evaluated on a control cell, and this note rather than the machine is what carries the guard's force on this row today. The engine change that would close that hole - an assertion that every declared basis_guard either matches at least one live register row or carries basis_guard_vacuous_by_design, failing the build otherwise - is recorded as a tooling gap and is outside this config's scope.

utensils-plastic-silicone-tools.name: Plastic/silicone tools
utensils-plastic-silicone-tools.native_basis: specific element migration into food or food simulant (µg/kg food), Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II convention
utensils-plastic-silicone-tools.native_basis_label: specific element migration INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT from the polymeric food-contact surface, µg/kg of food, determined by the Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex III to V simulant, temperature and contact-time conventions. This is a MIGRATION basis and not a total-content basis: no cell on this row limits how much of an element the material CONTAINS, and no cell on this row is expressed per kg of material.
utensils-plastic-silicone-tools.scope_note: Hand tools whose food-contact head is a polymer. Plastic heads are articles consisting exclusively of plastics and are directly within Reg (EU) 10/2011; SILICONE heads are excluded from that instrument by its Art. 2(2)(c) and take the identical ceilings by disclosed read-across, which changes no published number. The distinguishing contact condition is short, repeated, HIGH-TEMPERATURE contact against a hot pan surface, well above the ambient migration convention, so the release test must be run at the tool's stated maximum service temperature and after the declared thermal cycling. Bonded metal cores are metal components under the alloy-release regime. Because that read-across is a real provenance difference rather than a wording nuance, every published cell on this row now carries READ-ACROSS provenance rather than regulatory-alignment, and each cell's label and substantiation name which configuration the instrument governs directly and which takes the value by read-across. food-prep-coffee-maker-pathways.scope_note: The full WETTED PATHWAY of a beverage-brewing appliance, from reservoir to cup, taken as a system rather than as a single material. The row is a control because the pathway is dominated by components in material families for which no credible sovereign sets an element release ceiling: aluminium and copper boilers, brass and leaded-brass fittings and group heads, and plated wetted parts. Two conditions make this row harsher than a storage article and are written into the component plan: the water is HOT and often near-boiling and is held in contact with the boiler and fittings, and DESCALING with acid is a manufacturer-instructed periodic condition that strips passivation and mobilises metal, so the release test must include a post-descaling draw. Polymeric reservoirs, carafes and tubing are bound by the plastics migration ceilings directly or by disclosed read-across as separate components, and the sovereign drinking-water parametric values are disclosed as WATER-basis companions on the beverage, never as this row's release ceilings. TRACEABILITY OF THE COMPONENT POINTER: where this row's component plan refers a plastic component to "the plastics migration ceilings", that phrase resolves to a concrete published set of values inside this same standard and is not an unresolved pointer. It means the Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II values published on this category's plastics rows — eu_10_2011_pb_sml_nd (lead, not detectable at 10 ug/kg food), eu_10_2011_cd_sml_nd (cadmium, 2), eu_10_2011_tas_sml_nd (total arsenic, 10), eu_10_2011_thg_sml_nd (total mercury, 10), eu_10_2011_ni_sml (nickel, 20), eu_10_2011_al_sml (aluminium, 1000) and eu_10_2011_crtotal_sml_nd (total chromium, not detectable at 10), with tin excepted because the instrument lists no tin entry. Those values bind the plastic component as a SEPARATE obligation in its own material family and are never this row's published ceiling, which stays in this row's own native basis.

food-prep-coffee-maker-pathways.basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as element RELEASE from a metal or alloy food-contact surface into food or a food simulant may anchor a cell on this row. The guard exists to reject the three foreign bases that surround this category and would otherwise look plausible: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents and not the article), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (CPSIA total lead in substrate, EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium percent-by-weight restrictions, RoHS homogeneous-material limits, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals), and the ARTICLE-EXTRACTION basis of the toy regime (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III and ASTM F963 soluble limits, which are element migration from scraped-off or coated TOY material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid, expressed per kg of MATERIAL, not per kg of food). Any of those would fail this guard and resolve to a gap rather than publish in the wrong basis. On this control row the guard is declaratory as well as operative: it records the only basis in which a future ingested instrument would be allowed to supply this row's numbers, so that a content limit, a food limit, a water limit or a plastics specific migration limit cannot later be dropped in as this row's release ceiling. The plastics clause is deliberately absent from this guard: a Reg (EU) 10/2011 value named here would fail the guard and resolve to a gap. DECLARED VACUOUS STATE (recorded, not overlooked): as written this guard matches ZERO live, non-draft and non-quarantined rows in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv, and that is its intended state. The release regime this row's basis family belongs to is not in the register in any form this row may bind, which is the same fact this row's control cells record and state in detail; a guard that admitted a live row today could only do so by admitting a foreign basis. The guard is nevertheless expressed in the register's own basis vocabulary (element or specific release, release into food or a food simulant, 4 percent acetic acid extract, per dm2 of food-contact surface, net device contribution to the treated water) so that a future correct ingest of that regime BINDS through it. food-prep-kettle-interiors.name: Kettle interiors
food-prep-kettle-interiors.native_basis: element release from the food-contact alloy into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
food-prep-kettle-interiors.native_basis_label: element RELEASE FROM THE FOOD-CONTACT ALLOY INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT, µg/kg of food, determined against an acidic simulant at the article's stated use temperature and duration with the third successive release governing for repeat-use articles. This is a RELEASE basis on the food, not the plastics-simulant convention and not a total-content basis: the percent-by-weight lead limits on food-contact metals and solder are a separate MATERIAL-CONTENT obligation, disclosed as companions and never published here.
food-prep-kettle-interiors.scope_note: The interior wetted surface of an electric or stovetop kettle, taken at BOILING as the operative condition. The row is a control because the characteristic components sit in material families with no sovereign element release ceiling: the exposed heating element and its boss, brass and plated fittings, and welded seams. Boiling water contact is a harsher extraction than any of the standard food-simulant conventions and is the condition the test must use; repeated boil-dry cycles and periodic acid descaling are additional required conditionings. Plastic kettle bodies and lids are bound by the plastics migration ceilings as separate components; glass bodies fall to the glass-and-glaze control regime. TRACEABILITY OF THE COMPONENT POINTER: where this row's component plan refers a plastic component to "the plastics migration ceilings", that phrase resolves to a concrete published set of values inside this same standard and is not an unresolved pointer. It means the Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II values published on this category's plastics rows — eu_10_2011_pb_sml_nd (lead, not detectable at 10 ug/kg food), eu_10_2011_cd_sml_nd (cadmium, 2), eu_10_2011_tas_sml_nd (total arsenic, 10), eu_10_2011_thg_sml_nd (total mercury, 10), eu_10_2011_ni_sml (nickel, 20), eu_10_2011_al_sml (aluminium, 1000) and eu_10_2011_crtotal_sml_nd (total chromium, not detectable at 10), with tin excepted because the instrument lists no tin entry. Those values bind the plastic component as a SEPARATE obligation in its own material family and are never this row's published ceiling, which stays in this row's own native basis.
food-prep-kettle-interiors.material: Austenitic stainless-steel and borosilicate-glass kettle bodies; polypropylene and copolyester bodies and lids; exposed and concealed heating elements, nickel-plated or stainless; brass and plated fittings at the element boss, thermostat well and spout; welded seams; limescale-bearing interior surfaces in hard-water use.
food-prep-kettle-interiors.components: Sample and report separately: (1) first-boil and repeat-boil water sampling from the assembled kettle against a matched influent blank, at the rated fill and at minimum fill; (2) exposed HEATING ELEMENT surface and its boss or gland, including any plating and any braze; (3) brass and plated fittings at the element boss, thermostat well, sight glass and spout; (4) welds, seams and any solder; (5) POST-DESCALING boil, immediately after the stated descaling procedure and again after the stated flush; (6) plastic body, lid, filter and spout components under the plastics migration ceilings; (7) glass bodies as their own lot under the glass-and-glaze control regime.

food-prep-kettle-interiors.basis_guard: element release|specific release|specific release limit|release into food|release into a food simulant|release into the food simulant|acetic acid
food-prep-kettle-interiors.basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as element RELEASE from a metal or alloy food-contact surface into food or a food simulant may anchor a cell on this row. The guard exists to reject the three foreign bases that surround this category and would otherwise look plausible: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents and not the article), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (CPSIA total lead in substrate, EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium percent-by-weight restrictions, RoHS homogeneous-material limits, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals), and the ARTICLE-EXTRACTION basis of the toy regime (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III and ASTM F963 soluble limits, which are element migration from scraped-off or coated TOY material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid, expressed per kg of MATERIAL, not per kg of food). Any of those would fail this guard and resolve to a gap rather than publish in the wrong basis. On this control row the guard is declaratory as well as operative: it records the only basis in which a future ingested instrument would be allowed to supply this row's numbers, so that a content limit, a food limit, a water limit or a plastics specific migration limit cannot later be dropped in as this row's release ceiling. The plastics clause is deliberately absent from this guard: a Reg (EU) 10/2011 value named here would fail the guard and resolve to a gap. DECLARED VACUOUS STATE (recorded, not overlooked): as written this guard matches ZERO live, non-draft and non-quarantined rows in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv, and that is its intended state. The release regime this row's basis family belongs to is not in the register in any form this row may bind, which is the same fact this row's control cells record and state in detail; a guard that admitted a live row today could only do so by admitting a foreign basis. The guard is nevertheless expressed in the register's own basis vocabulary (element or specific release, release into food or a food simulant, 4 percent acetic acid extract, per dm2 of food-contact surface, net device contribution to the treated water) so that a future correct ingest of that regime BINDS through it. water-filters.native_basis_label: NET ELEMENT RELEASE FROM THE TREATMENT DEVICE INTO THE TREATED WATER, µg/L reported as µg/kg, determined as device effluent minus a matched influent blank so that any contribution BY the device is resolved separately from what the device removes. water-filters.scope_note: The assembled point-of-use treatment device.
